#5670. California Voters Could Approve ‘Secondary Mortgages.’ Can the Golden State Solve the Housing Crisis?

Lawmakers and advocates have made many attempts recently to address the affordability crisis that pervades the housing market—some more impactful than others. Legislative bodies have enacted laws addressing private listings, while President Donald Trump recently signed an executive order aimed at cutting costs for title and mortgage insurance and manufactured housing.

In tomorrow’s general election, California voters will vote on a meaningful and unique new measure that essentially allows first-time buyers to borrow the bulk of their down payment, theoretically removing a big barrier to homeownership (with several caveats).

California Proposition 37—or the Second Mortgage Homebuyer Program and Revenue Bond Initiative—would create an assistance program for first-time homebuyers, offering them loans that could cover up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, meaning a buyer only needs to put 3% down to reach the 20% threshold needed to avoid mortgage insurance.

One of the primary sponsors of the initiative, former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg spoke with RISMedia and desired for more California residents to achieve homeownership.

“We’re really underhoused in California, so much of the focus has been on subsidized tax supported rental housing. I don’t take that away for a second, but we haven’t done a really good job at making sure that middle-class folks—the missing middle—are able to buy a house,” he says.

The initiative would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in bonds to offer secondary mortgage loans for down payments, to eligible buyers.

To qualify for the program, applicants must have been residents of California for at least one year, agree to occupy the home as a primary residence within 60 days of closing, fall under the middle-income buyer threshold and provide a down payment of no less than 3% of the purchase price of the qualified homes.

The proposition is aimed at “middle-income buyers,” or buyers who have an income at or below 200% of the area median income.

A qualified home includes any “newly constructed homes, townhouses, row houses, condominiums, or manufactured homes, or a condominium or other residence in a nonresidential building repurposed for residential use, where the borrower is the first purchaser,” according to the proposition.

Within these limitations, the program theoretically allows buyers to put down much less while still getting the keys (the 3% down payment still comes out to around $17,000 for a median-priced new home in the state).

As for the $25 billion in bonds, Hertzberg emphasizes that funding does not rely on taxpayer wallets, but rather investors. What’s more, the bonds will be recycled continuously.

“The bottom line is, it’s evergreen. Evergreen means that it’s not over. When you pay off the loan, it’s evergreen and the money goes back out to somebody else,” Hertzberg notes. “Thirty years from now when all these initial loans are paid off, there’ll be brand new loans. We hired a professor from UCLA who analyzed it and said that it’ll raise $150 billion in new construction and 190,000 new homes.”

Michael Lane—state policy director at the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association (SPUR)—approves the initiative because it focuses on new homes.

“There are some programs the state has implemented which are just down payment assistance programs without creating new housing,” he asserts. “You’re actually just creating—with those programs—more demand for the existing housing stock, which means more competition which will also boost prices. We think it’s important for this to focus on new construction as well as the down payment assistance.”

Within the proposition, a “secondary mortgage” is a somewhat unique concept. In this case, a secondary mortgage refers to the loan offered to qualified homebuyers, of which goes toward a home’s down payment.

“This is different from a second mortgage,” David Garcia, deputy director of Policy at the Terner Center for Housing Innovation UC Berkeley, stated.

A website made by supporters of the proposition contains a tool that allows voters to view median home price by each county in California, and uses data provided by the California Association of Realtors®.

As with many coastal states, California has a divided housing market. According to the latest data, California metros were not immune to the effects of elevated mortgage rates, as pending home sales fell even in high activity cities such as San Francisco and San Jose.

Construction has fared no better, as the latest report from The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Census Bureau shows that housing starts in the West are down over 23% monthly, and down 25% from the previous year.

In that context, Proposition 37 is particularly relevant as the state seeks to sustainably increase housing that is affordable in a market that is both land constrained and highly regulated.

“We’re also focused on construction defect liability reform and liquidated damages for condominiums in California,” Lane notes. “We’re at a disadvantage compared to other states; it makes it more risky to build condominiums here. That’s why we don’t produce very many—about 3,000 developments of five units or more—compared to other states and nations which do 10 times that amount with lesser populations.”

Homebuilders cite global tensions and labor shortages for faltering construction rates. Although the conclusion of each year typically ushers in a slowdown in housing activity, the latest data for new-home sales showcases further deceleration, likely caused by high mortgage rates and economic unease.

The Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley does not take positions on bills or legislation. But Garcia does note that the initiative may encourage more than buyers.

“By limiting the use of funds to newly built housing, it also may act as an incentive for builders to build more homes that are for sale,” he says.

Although his focus is on housing in Sacramento, Lane points out that California’s homeownership rates leave much to be desired.

“We have one of the lowest homeownership rates in the nation here in California because of our high housing costs and the median home price of over $800,000; it makes it very difficult for working families to scrape together the 20% down payment,” he notes.

Notably, California is one of only a few states where new homes are cheaper than existing homes, making Proposition 37 potentially more powerful at addressing affordability.

Lane also believes that more changes to California’s housing market will come, specifically by drawing investors and builders to the state.

“We’ve been working on this issue for decades and will continue to do so; there’s always more to do,” Lane says. “In California, the cost of construction and the rules for project approvals can make it very difficult and time-consuming. That’s why investors oftentimes look for other opportunities rather than investing in housing in California. We’ll continue to make it more business-friendly and friendly for housing construction.”

With five years’ worth of work nearing its climax, Hertzberg states that his goal with Prop 37 is to encourage the supply of affordable homes, in the hopes of addressing California’s low homeownership rates.

“It’s the simplest rule in economics, supply and demand,” he adds. “You get more supply, it works better. People can say all the arguments they want to make, but we don’t have enough middle-class housing.”

Despite his retirement, Hertzberg noted that he’s met with a handful of opposing groups, but states that many arguments against the initiative have not “done their homework.”

The League of Women Voters in California (LWV) declined to speak with RISMedia on the proposition, but they are opposed to it. The group’s argument is that the proposition essentially adds a second mortgage for buyers to repay, alongside their primary mortgage, each month.

“The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers,” the LWV’s voting recommendations state. “Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3% of the home price.”

The LWV also stated that voters would not know the interest rate, loan term or monthly payment amount prior to the program’s approval. Essentially, the LWV argues that the program would put homeowners in more debt.

Hertzberg rejected these notions, responding that the group’s arguments are “ridiculous” and that with purchase money security interest (PMSI), the only players to take a loss should there be a significant downturn in home prices are the banks and bondholders.

“PMSI means that there is no liability,” Hertzberg claims. “Assume we had a downturn, where a home’s value drops significantly. The bank and the bondholders take the loss. The only thing that the buyer loses if they buy a house for $900,000, is $30,000. There’s no downside risk beyond losing your down payment.”

He also emphasizes the safeguards the initiative includes, in reference to the 2008 financial crisis that rocked the world.

“People in 2008 had variable-rate mortgages. Their mortgage went from $1,200 to $2,400, and they couldn’t afford it. These down payment loans are fixed-rate mortgages. For renters, I promise you this much: In 10 years your rent’s going up. That doesn’t happen in a fixed-rate mortgage,” Hertzberg stresses.

While it may not be the optimal option for all first-time homebuyers, Garcia does acknowledge that some buyers in California may find use out of the program.

“I think it’s useful in a circumstance where a homebuyer or family has the income to cover the payments for both a first and second mortgage, but don’t have the liquidity,” he says. “It’s just an alternative pathway for individuals who just don’t have a lot of cash on hand to afford homeownership.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5669. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5668. Project-by-project security reviews can’t keep pace with enterprise AI agents

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are finding that tokenization and other data protection methods now decide how fast those projects move.

But sensitive data fed into models is hard to pull back — and security reviews built for a slower era are stalling deployments. The challenge is shifting from locking data down to keeping it usable once it is protected. That tension is playing out across Cloudera Inc.’s partner ecosystem, where security is becoming a prerequisite for AI value rather than a final gate, according to Diego Loureda (pictured), vice president of customer success and presales at Protegrity USA Inc.

“Data leaks are still a thing. If you put sensitive data on a model, if you put sensitive data on a vector store or in the memory of an agent that is going to propagate to other agents, good luck removing that sensitive data,” Loureda said. “There’s no way you’re going to be able to do that.”

Loureda spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed data security along with Protegrity being named Cloudera’s Emerging Technology Partner of the Year. (* Disclosure below.)

Traditional encryption can lock data so tightly that analysts and models can no longer use it. Protegrity centers its approach on tokenization, which swaps sensitive values for substitutes instead of relying on a mathematical algorithm, Loureda explained. That design also matters as quantum computing threatens today’s cryptography.

“Our main method of protection, that is tokenization, it’s already quantum ready,” Loureda said. “The reason behind that is because there is no mathematical algorithm behind it. It’s all based on replacement in memory.”

Protection alone doesn’t solve the speed problem, however. In research Protegrity commissioned from Enterprise Management Associates Inc., 83% of leaders reported project delays, Loureda noted.

“The main problem with governance is that companies are approving projects and that will not scale in the age of AI,” Loureda said. “They have to approve patterns.”

The same study found 82% of leaders push agents into production in a diminished state, stripped of the tools and data that would make them useful, he added. Controls such as tokenization let security teams clear the way for those agents instead, according to Loureda.

“Security has always been the business of no, the department of no. That changes now,” he said. “These days security is the team that can enable AI to give you value.”

#5667. Rebecca Gayheart Reveals Shock of Eric Dane’s Death—and How They Made His Hospital Room Feel Like Home in His Final Moments

Eric Dane's estranged wife, Rebecca Gayheart, has lifted the lid on the shock that came with the actor's death, revealing that she had "no idea that was it."

While speaking to NBC's Maria Shriver on Nov. 3—the same day the late Hollywood star's memoir, "My Book of Days," hit shelves—Gayheart, 55, reflected on the final moments of Dane's life.

The actor, was diagnosed with the degenerative neurological disease in April 2025 and died on the afternoon of Feb. 19, 2026. Gayheart confessed that she and their two daughters, Billie and Georgia, "never, ever anticipated" that he would pass away when he did.

“He had gone to the hospital so many times before, and they would patch him up, so to speak, and he would come home,” Gayheart explained. “And he’d be OK. And we’d go back to the normal routine, which did change week by week.”

She then recalled her estranged husband's first day in the hospital during his first trip there.

“I said, ‘Listen, I’ll be back. I have a dinner. I’m going to this event.’ I had no idea that that was it, that that week was going to be our last week,” Gayheart revealed. “And nor did my daughters. It really took a few days for us to understand the gravity of what that last trip to the hospital meant.”

She noted that she and their daughters began to realize how bad things had become a few days into the hospital visit.

“I think it was like day three in the hospital where it shifted. Everything shifted. Just the tone of when the doctors were talking to us, and some of the information we were given," Gayheart said.

At the same time, Dane was also beginning to come to terms with his last days.

“He was fully aware it was shifting, and he was still communicating with us. Not well verbally, but I could understand him most of the time. The kids could most of the time, his closest friends," she revealed.

Meanwhile, friends of Dane and Gayheart helped her through the emotional turmoil as she struggled with "decision fatigue."

“It was figuring it out as we went, but I remember the moment Eric decided to make some choices, and he did. ... He was in control of the way he was going to leave," she said.

Because they couldn't set up their usual family sleepover at home, they brought everything they needed to the hospital to ensure they could spend Dane's final moments with him.

“The girls and I just camped out there with him, and we had our family sleepovers, and we brought in those little candles that aren’t real candles. They have batteries. And we played his favorite music, and we tried to make it as nice as you can be in the hospital room," she revealed.

Although they cherished their final moments with Dane, Gayheart revealed she wasn't prepared for how quickly the time to say goodbye came.

“A lot of people will say, ‘Well, at least you knew, and you could have those last conversations.' But we didn’t know, because there is no road map. No one can tell you what the journey looks like because it’s so different for every patient. He was becoming more alive mentally, but losing all of his physical abilities. And for the girls, that was really hard to watch as well. But overall, it’s a blur, because it was just so overwhelming," she said.

Dane was meant to meet with Shriver shortly before his death; however, they had to reschedule their plans because the actor wasn't feeling well and mere days later, Dane died.

In Dane's memoir, which was released Nov. 3, he revealed he was initially diagnosed with multifocal motor neuropathy, a treatable autoimmune condition, just months before he received his ALS diagnosis.

Speaking about the book, Gayheart previously told People, she was “grateful he did, because it gives my girls the opportunity to know their dad as a human being.”

In the days leading up to his death, the family found comfort in familiar routines, eating sushi, watching movies, and gathering for game nights.

“We tried to be present through all of our fear and frustration and uncertainty. It was truly an exhausting and heartbreaking experience, but it also showed us his extraordinary strength every day, and that was really wonderful for the girls and myself to witness,” she told People.

In an excerpt previously published by the outlet, Dane recalled the devastating phone call in which he told Gayheart about his diagnosis.

“I say to Rebecca on the phone, ‘It’s what we feared.’ I don’t remember a single word I said after that,” he wrote.

Despite their separation, Dane made clear that he and Gayheart remained a family.

The “Grey’s Anatomy” actor described the news as a “violent impact,” comparing the feeling to “getting the wind knocked out of me.”

As he struggled to process the diagnosis, he recalled hearing Gayheart “wailing on the other end of the phone.”

“My sobs make my body shudder, and I hear her words pouring out amid her tears, ‘I’m here, we’ll fight this together, I’m not going anywhere,’” he wrote.

Throughout the memoir, Dane described how his daughters gave him a sense of purpose as he faced the disease.

“I’m going to show my girls how to walk through this life with grace and dignity, no matter what. I am going to FIGHT. This has become my purpose. My reason. This is now my job,” he wrote.

Dane's death was revealed in a statement by his representatives.

“He spent his final days surrounded by dear friends, his devoted wife, and his two beautiful daughters, Billie and Georgia, who were the center of his world.

Following his death, many of his celebrity friends have come forward to lay bare the actor's final moments.

Dane and and Gayheart, 54, tied the knot in 2004, and share daughters Billie Beatrice, 15, and Georgia Geraldine, 13.

Gayheart filed for divorce from Dane in 2018. However, in March 2025, just one month before the "Grey's Anatomy" alum announced his diagnosis, she dismissed the filing.

While speaking on the podcast "Broad Ideas," Gayheart had opened up about the state of their relationship, insisting that she will always be there to support Dane, even though their marriage had ended.

“We’ve been separated for eight years. The kids live with me 100% of the time. There’s been lots of just stuff, other stuff,” she told hosts Rachel Bilson and Olivia Allen.

She added that it is important for her to be a "role model" for her daughters, particularly in how she treats her former spouse.

“I am definitely trying to show them that we show up for people, no matter what. He is our family. He is your father. We show up, and we try to do it with some dignity and some grace and just get through it and that we will get through it the best we can," she said.

Gayheart noted that she was staying afloat and helping her loved ones by trying to "stay optimistic."

ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a disorder that affects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord, according to the ALS Association.

For around 90% of cases of ALS, there is no known family history or a genetic mutation linked to ALS.

For 5% to 10% of cases, there is a family history of the disease. This is often referred to as familial ALS.

There is currently no known cure for ALS. However, there are FDA-approved medications that may help slow down the progression of the disease.

After sharing his diagnosis, Dane closely guarded many of the details of his medical battle.

According to his IMDB page, the actor had three projects that were due to be released: "Euphoria" Season 3, which premiered April 12, 2026; a 13-episode thriller called "Countdown"; and a movie called "Family Secrets."

Dane rose to stardom after appearing in ABC's hit medical drama "Grey's Anatomy," where he played the role of Dr. Mark Sloan, who was often referred to as "McSteamy."

At the time of his death, Dane was believed to be residing in a three-bedroom, three-bathroom pad that spans 2,265 square feet, which he snapped up with Gayheart in 2000 for $949,000.

#5666. Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work

Artificial intelligence agents have become two a penny in the enterprise today, but just because they’re rapidly being commoditized does not mean organizations know how best to use them.

That’s the challenge a startup called Marble Cognition is trying to solve after raising $3.75 million in pre-seed funding to coincide with its launch today. The round was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, and saw participation from angel investors that include executives from McKinsey & Co., Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog Inc.

Munich-based Marble was co-founded by the German AI engineers Felix Rösner (pictured, left) and Christophe Schmit (right), who were among the first to realize that AI agents have already become a commodity, used by almost every enterprise in some capacity or other. Most organizations are using AI agents primarily for writing software, but Rösner believes that to see the real value of those autonomous workers, companies need to provide them with the granular operational context that tells them what they actually need to build and automate.

But building this picture is a notoriously difficult challenge because few corporate workflows run according to neat blueprints. Though a study by McKinsey & Co. suggests that it’s theoretically possible to automate 57% of all work hours in the U.S., most companies haven’t gotten anywhere near that goal.

That’s because more than 90% of business processes live within things like messy email threads, scattered spreadsheets and inside the minds of employees. To teach AI agents what needs to be built and automated, companies need to piece all of those processes into a picture they can follow.

This is exactly the challenge Marble seeks to address. Its AI agents are designed to capture those business workflows at the source. The startup has developed a dedicated desktop application that sits and monitors how employees work using different tools and processes. It takes screenshots and captures worker’s clicks and keystrokes, before transforming this data into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, similar to code.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work,” Rösner said. “But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the same way your best people do.”

Once the data is gathered, Marble then deploys its Coworkers, which are designed to take over the most repetitive work processes from people and run them end-to-end an organization’s existing software stacks, with humans remaining in the loop when important decisions need to be made.

Rösner said Marble has already delivered some serious efficiency gains for early adopters like EGYM GmbH, Mutares SE & Co. KGaA and Enam GmbH. In the case of one private equity-backed U.S. financial services firm, Marble’s Coworkers were configured to create settlement offers for human review. As a result of that work, the company was able to slash its case-handling times by 90%, which meant that its human staffers could process around 50% more claims without needing to hire anyone else.

Seedcamp General Partner Reshma Sohoni, an early backer of the robotic process automation firm UiPath Inc., said the vast majority of companies in the world want to learn how to automate more of their work. “The hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done, so you can actually automate it,” he said. “Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future.”

#5665. Enterprises bring AI to their data as privacy rules tighten and costs climb

Every enterprise AI strategy eventually comes down to the same question: Should proprietary data travel to the model, or should the model come to the data?

“Rather than saying, ‘Just give us all your data and we’ll in return provide you access to a model that’s then contextualized based on that data,’ we turn things around,” Stoop said. “We say, ‘We’ll bring AI to where the data is and where the data lives.'”

Stoop spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can bring AI to their data while maintaining control and managing costs. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloudera’s latest move in that direction is a partnership with Mistral AI SAS, which brings Mistral’s models into Cloudera’s data platform. For European customers in particular, the model maker’s local roots matter as much as its technology, Stoop noted.

“Certainly for us in Europe, having a French organization, a local company, that provides these models and provides the complete stack is very attractive for a lot of our customers,” Stoop said. “Mistral was a very easy choice for us to say, ‘Those are the ones that we’re going with.'”

AI is at the top of a maturity curve that starts with sovereign data, sovereign cloud and local operations, according to Stoop. Rules such as the European Union’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and the U.S. CLOUD Act are pushing organizations to prove they have control rather than simply claim it. But control alone won’t move AI out of the pilot phase. For many companies, the bigger obstacle in an enterprise AI strategy is the cost of running models at scale, because generating tokens takes a lot of hardware.

“If you use a public provider for that, the more you use your model, the more you get hit on cost,” Stoop said. “How do I get that high utilization of a good model inside my organization without being exposed to horrific costs? That, I think, is the biggest challenge that organizations are struggling with right now.”

#5664. Trump Remains ‘Laser-Focused’ on Housing Affordability Despite Final Midterm Speech on DC Reflecting Pool, White House Says

In his final message to voters ahead to the pivotal midterm elections, President Donald Trump touted renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool without uttering a word about housing affordability. Still, the White House says he remains squarely focused on the issue.

"President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Realtor.com® in a statement.

Ingle noted that Trump in his second term had signed an executive order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and "cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs."

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," he said.

During his speech on Monday evening by the reflecting pool in the heart of Washington, DC, Trump spoke at length and in exhaustive detail about the extensive repairs to leaky pipes, surface coating, and cracked granite.

"This is a massive piece of pool," Trump told an audience of several dozen people gathered for the unveiling of the refurbished monument, which has been one of his signature projects since the opening months of his second term.

Trump reiterated claims that the pool had been vandalized by "sick" saboteurs. However, federal prosecutors and the U.S. Attorney's Office for DC previously acknowledged in court filings that the damage to the pool lining that accompanied massive algae blooms was the product of shoddy installation by contractors rushing to complete the job before the 250th Independence Day festivities.

Beyond his breakdown of the pool makeover, which is projected to cost taxpayers about $16 million, Trump touted his record in his second White House term, claiming that his administration had reduced crime in DC by "close to 90%," carried out sweeping beautification projects, and cleared out homeless encampments.

It was not until 23 minutes into his address that Trump finally mentioned the looming midterm election, which will determine control of Congress and could shape the final two years of his time in the White House.

"This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm, I believe in our lifetime," said the president.

The stakes could hardly be higher: control of the U.S. Senate and House, dozens of governorships, crucial ballot measures on housing, and the legislative direction of the second half of Trump's term.

Final preelection polling showed Democrats holding a meaningful advantage in the generic congressional ballot and leading in several key Senate battlegrounds, including Michigan, Texas, and Maine, driven by widespread voter frustration with the surging costs of fuel, groceries, and housing.

While Trump did not bring up affordability in his remarks, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who joined him at the event in DC, briefly touched upon the subject, arguing that Trump's policies have paved the way to "food security, more grazing for our country, more timber production for affordable homes, and more oil and gas to drive the price and affordability of energy down in our country."

This fall, average 30-year mortgage rates surged back past the 7% mark, propelled by surging oil prices linked to the president's ongoing war in Iran, severely eroding homebuyers' purchasing power.

The broader cost-of-living squeeze has not gone unnoticed by the electorate across the political spectrum, prompting Trump to hit the campaign trail in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas and South Carolina to shore up support for vulnerable GOP candidates.

Yet in his concluding remarks on the eve of the election, the president struck an uncharacteristically fatalistic tone and appeared resigned to a potential "blue wave."

"Usually whoever the sitting president is—Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad—for some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms," he said. "But we gave this a very strong shot."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5663. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5662. Offerpad CEO: Market Issues Main Cause of Glum Q3 Performance

In a Q3 2026 earnings report Nov. 2, iBuyer Offerpad, known for giving homeowners cash offers within 24 hours, blamed the less-than-stout housing market for its less-than-stout numbers.

In a release and press conference, the company reported a net loss of $11.5 million, or $2.30 a share—with total closed real estate transactions numbering 324. Gross profit was $6.5 million, with a gross margin of 8.3%. Contribution profit after interest per real estate transaction was approximately $12,900, near Q2 levels and about double the prior-year quarter.

On the plus side, the 324 real estate transactions were up from 295 in the second quarter and 263 in the first quarter, marking a steady sequential recovery in activity.

Brian Bair, Offerpad’s chairman and CEO, explained that high mortgage rates and slowing buyer demand were the main culprits for the lackluster Q3 performance.

“Mortgage rates rose more than 70 basis points from mid-August to early October, putting additional pressure on housing affordability and slowing buyer demand,” he said. “As homes took longer to sell, we adjusted our acquisition criteria to require higher expected returns and became more selective about new purchases, while serving more sellers through Cash Offer Marketplace and Brokerage Services. Having multiple ways to serve homeowners gives us flexibility to keep growing transactions while maintaining capital discipline.”

“Our focus is converting inventory into cash and continuing to optimize our cost base,” added Andrew Pieper, interim CFO. “Together, we expect those actions to continue to support liquidity and lower the transaction volume required to reach Adjusted EBITDA breakeven.”

Offerpad shares closed the regular session at $2.07, down 4.61% from the previous close of $2.17. In after-hours trading, the stock dipped to $2.05, down 0.97% from the close. From the prior day’s close to the after-hours quote, the shares were down around 5.5%. The stock is trading near the low end of its 52-week range of $2.06 to $26.70, showing how far investor sentiment has weakened over the past year.

Questioned after the formal conference about the current home seller mentality, Bair noted that it has for sure changed.

“We have seen this thing evolve over the last several years, but I think this is the very first time that a majority of the sellers know it is a buyer’s market,” he said. “They are seeing active listings around their areas continue to increase. The good part about that is that we can buy at wider margins and be more selective about what we are acquiring.

“Of course, what we have to be very sensitive to is making sure that we are buying the right type of product in the right areas. We are continuing to stick with the interior homes. The outlying areas are definitely impacted more than most areas. Our portfolio still consists of interior homes, newer, not as much renovation. Of course, we still have renovation, but the $100,000 renovation projects that we have done in the past, we are not looking at doing right now.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5661. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5660. With Agentic Studio, LinearB provides the critical context needed to accelerate software delivery

Application development intelligence startup LinearB Inc. said today it’s trying to ease the growing congestion in organization’s software delivery pipelines that has arisen with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence coding tools.

It’s doing so with Agentic Studio, a new offering announced today that’s focused on providing more actionable context for human engineers and autonomous coding agents alike.

The startup says the emergence of generative AI coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex has led to new headaches for enterprise software development teams. Though writing software code now can be basically effortless, shipping that code into production is still as painful as it has always been, and now they have much more of it to ship.

In its recent Software Engineering Benchmarks report, the company analyzed more than 2.7 million pull requests across 250 organizations and found that those who rely on AI coding tools have almost doubled their merged code changes year-over-year. But the problem is that AI-assisted pull requests are nearly 2.6 times larger, and consequently they’re waiting more than five times longer to be reviewed.

That has led to significant backlogs. And it’s compounded by the fact that AI agent’s proposed code changes are merged just 79% of the time at “elite organizations,” compared with 92% for human-authored code.

LinearB says that human software engineers struggle to clear this backlog because the traditional dashboards they’re forced to work with only provide metrics, rather than the context needed to resolve those pull requests. With Agentic Studio, it’s trying to address this by normalizing the data and insights generated by Git repositories and project tracking tools into a unified context layer. It means that instead of muddling through various charts to try and understand why release velocity has stalled, software engineers can ask questions in plain language to understand the root cause and receive recommendations on how to speed things up.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Ori Keren said context has become the new king, not only for AI tools but also for humans. “We realized we hold a knowledge graph that nobody else has of everything that is happening across the software delivery lifecycle,” he said. “That’s exactly what agents and teams need to deliver high quality software faster, so we rebuilt LinearB around it.”

What’s different about Agentic Studio is that it’s designed to help autonomous coding agents just as much as human software engineers, Keren said. By integrating through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol, it feeds historical context such as rework rates, past production incidents and code ownership to AI agents, preventing them from making blind modifications to pull requests.

Early adopters have benefited from dramatically increased productivity with Agentic Studio. A case in point is the cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, which used LinearB’s MCP integration to pinpoint why its code reviews were lagging. It discovered that timezone misalignments were the main culprit rather than pull request sizes, and subsequently reorganized its workflows to cut its review times by more than half within just four months.

“For years, engineering leaders told us the same thing: metrics are useful, but they don’t tell you what to do,” said LinearB’s chief operating officer Dan Lines. “A dashboard says your cycle time is two days, but so what? Now [with Agentic Studio] a leader can ask what to improve in their engineering organization and get a clear answer. When that same context goes to coding agents, the platform is not just reporting, it’s acting.”

To help AI agents operationalize the context it provides, LinearB is developing a bunch of new agent skills. The first one, an “effort skill,” is available in early access now and analyzes the complexity of a pull request and its proposed code changes, its rework history and risk to calibrate dynamically how much computational effort a coding agent needs to expend as it works on it.

Simple, low-risk changes are done faster with minimal tokens. More sensitive, high-priority modifications will be implemented with deeper reasoning and more exhaustive testing to ensure nothing goes wrong.

LinearB said it’s planning to expand its agent skills library in the coming months with additional skills focused on automated code review, merge governance and token cost optimization.

#5658. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Find a New Home Base in the Cotswolds

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have reportedly moved into a new Cotswolds home on their friend's estate.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who moved to the U.K. in August with their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, have been settling into their new lives across the pond.

After making the move, the couple was living "in the main house" of their pal's sprawling property.

However, now, their living situation has reportedly changed, with the Daily Mail reporting that they have moved onto another property "on the estate."

According to the outlet, the friend is a wealthy businessman who Harry, 42, befriended through their mutual support for various charities.

Harry and Markle were rumored to have been house hunting, with several reports noting that the former actress was even looking to replicate the luxury they had in their Montecito mansion.

The duchess reportedly wants the U.K. residence to boast nine bedrooms—the same number as their California estate—as well as plenty of luxurious amenities.

The news of their move came mere weeks after Harry opened up about their decision to leave California behind  and relocate their family to the U.K., revealing that their children's education and his desire to reconnect with his roots played a major role in the decision.

In an interview with GQ that was filmed in September but released only recently, Harry explained that the opportunity to enroll his children in British schools was particularly meaningful to him.

“Opportunities for the family, being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn’t know how important it was to me,” he said.

“I always thought it was going to be something that I would try to do or that we would try to do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it, and it’s just giving them a whole different experience.”

Harry emphasized that his decision was not a criticism of the U.S. education system, but rather an opportunity for Archie and Lilibet to experience life in two different countries.

“I’m not criticizing American schools, but I think for kids at 7 and 5 to be able to have that comparison and to have two completely different cultural experiences is so important today,” he explained.

Beyond their education, Harry said returning to Britain has allowed his children to spend more time with relatives and develop closer relationships with family friends.

Another motivation for the move, he explained, was to “be back closer to my family and to be back on U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there.

“It’s been nice to be close to friends, family, friends and friends and their children as well, to be able to have endless playdates to really, like, help our kids settle in," he said.

Despite the significance of the relocation, Harry admitted that he and Meghan, 45, had not necessarily mapped out the move years in advance.

“For us, when certain stars align, and it’s clear that this should or probably will end up being the case, then we lean into that,” he said.

After spending six years living in California, he said he increasingly wanted his children to become familiar with the country where he spent his own childhood.

“Having been here for six years now and only being able to go back to the U.K. for short periods of time, to actually have my whole family there with me, the place that I grew up, wanting to be able to show my kids where I grew up and have them have the experiences to some extent that I had—the good rather than necessarily the bad—provided real, proper, serious thinking as to, ‘This is an opportunity, let’s do it now,’” he said.

Harry also addressed his complicated history with the British press, expressing hope that his family's return could mark the beginning of a more positive chapter.

“Once you’ve been through it, once you’ve been able to talk about it and raise awareness to it, then people see it for what it is, which makes the environment slightly easier,” he said.

“And it’s not going to necessarily stop the behavior, but then that’s the second part, which is the behavior: My hope is that it will change.”

The duke acknowledged that tensions have persisted in the years since he and Meghan stepped back from their roles as senior working royals, but suggested he would welcome an opportunity to move forward.

“What happened back then was then, what’s happened over the last six years has been a continuation of that. There are some battles that have been fought, necessarily so. But hopefully we can all draw a line under that,” he said.

He added that he hopes both his family and the British media can put certain disputes behind them.

“I am optimistic. I’m hopeful,” Harry said. “I’m not naive. I have been naive in the past. But I think it’s important to remain optimistic.”

The interview surfaced just days after Harry and Meghan made their first official joint appearance in the U.K. since their relocation.

On Oct. 15, the couple traveled to Nottingham, England, where they greeted approximately 100 people during a public engagement.

The pair also spent time interacting with local schoolchildren, crouching down to speak with them. Meghan was presented with flowers and a balloon during the visit.

"It's great to be back," she told one person.

The warm welcome was filled with several special moments, including one that saw the crowd shouting, "I love you Duchess Meghan."

The appearance marked their return to a city that played an important role in their early relationship, having served as the location of their first official joint engagement following their November 2017 engagement announcement.

Their outing came days after it was reported that they were turning their attention to their professional and charitable commitments after spending their first several weeks in Britain adjusting to their new surroundings.

Their latest chapter comes more than six years after the couple stepped away from their roles as working members of the royal family and established a new life in North America.

The visit came as an insider close to the couple told People that Harry and Meghan are eager to devote more attention to their philanthropic endeavors, having initially concentrated on helping their children adapt to living in a new country.

Their transition has not been without complications.

According to the outlet, Archie and Lilibet were forced to change schools just two days into the academic year due to security and logistical concerns surrounding their commute.

However, the children have reportedly adapted to their new environment, allowing their parents to devote additional time to commitments outside the family home.

A source told People that Harry and Meghan have established a schedule centered around their children's school hours, while continuing to prioritize spending time together as a family.

#5657. Court Report: NAR Fires Back in Compass Subpoena Spat; Keller Williams Sued for ‘Junk Fees’

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

NAR defends Compass subpoena in private listing lawsuit

The latest dust-up in the battle between now defunct PLS.com and the National Association of Realtors® (NAR) continues, as both parties await a judge’s decision on whether Compass can be compelled to provide witness and other evidence in the case.

Last week, a filing from NAR’s attorneys outlines the association’s opposition to a motion—by Compass, which is a non-party in the case—to quash subpoenas issued by NAR.

Within the memorandum, NAR argues that “Compass wants to supply PLS a friendly Compass witness while simultaneously, and blanketly, refusing to produce any documents for fair cross-examination. That hand-picked witness is Compass’s Chief Strategy Officer, Ashton Alexander.”

After significant back-and-forth, it appeared that NAR had dropped its demand to depose Compass CEO Robert Reffkin, but the two sides continue to wrangle over other witnesses—including rank-and-file Compass agents—as well as document requests that Compass has described as overly broad and “burdensome.”

“As outlined in our court filing, the petitioners cannot provide a witness to testify in support of PLS while simultaneously refusing to produce documents necessary for NAR to fairly cross-examine its witness,” an NAR spokesperson told RISMedia.

The association also argues that through various email threads, Reffkin and Alexander coordinated with PLS co-founder Mauricio Umansky in a “quest” against NAR’s Clear Cooperation Policy (CCP). PLS first sued NAR (and big MLSs) way back in 2020, settling with the MLSs and temporarily dropping the case against NAR before reviving it last year.

NAR’s court filings included emailed exchanges between Compass executives and Umansky over the last two years, including Reffkin sharing an op-ed slamming Clear Cooperation ahead of publication, and talking points on the policy ahead of both men attending an industry conference in early 2025.

In a joint filing from Compass and NAR, the brokerage argued that subpoenaing six non-party witnesses—including Reffkin, Alexander and Compass President of Integrated Services Cory Perkins—is “unduly burdensome on its face.”

NAR’s subpoenas focus on communications with clients and how those clients want to list their homes for sale, documents about membership in real estate trade association and other communications that Compass argues NAR should also possess.

So far, Compass stated that NAR is retaliating against Compass because one executive agreed to provide a deposition testimony for PLS.

NAR, on the other hand, argues that Alexander’s deposition and the documents it requested could implicate the testimony or documents of the other Compass-affiliated agents.

“The stakes are high,” NAR’s argument states.

The association’s explanations for the subpoenas also touch upon requests for further information from Compass, specifically information that PLS cannot provide.

“(The documents the parties themselves have produced) do not entail the Compass-affiliated agents’ listing agreements, which would reflect seller opt-outs of the MLS, or show whether off-MLS marketing was driven by seller preference or the agent’s business objectives. The bare listing information that PLS produced does not absolve Compass of its duties; PLS, for example, never tracked sales data,” NAR’s argument states.

Both parties, and Compass as a non-party, await a judge’s decision on whether the brokerage will have to provide the subpoenaed documents and communications.

Another player enters Compass MLS lawsuits

The Northern California-based MLS, MLSListings, announced that it has joined six MLSs in their federal lawsuit against Compass.

The six other MLSs in the lawsuit alongside MLSListings are Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service (ARMLS), BridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS and REcolorado.

Two other MLSs—OneKey and CRMLS—are suing Compass in a separate but largely identical lawsuit. All of the MLS’ appeared to have received legal threats from Compass back in September, focused on listing restrictions.

According to the amended complaint, the lawsuit arises from a “campaign by Compass to pressure MLSs into changing cooperation rules in a way that would favor Compass but would make the market for residential real estate less transparent and less competitive, ultimately hurting consumers.”

“In Silicon Valley and throughout Northern California, buyers, sellers and real estate professionals depend on timely, accurate information to make important financial decisions,” MLSListings President and CEO Dave Wetzel said. “When publicly marketed homes are withheld from the shared marketplace, buyers lose access to opportunities, sellers may miss potential offers, and smaller brokerages are placed at a disadvantage. We are joining this lawsuit to defend the cooperation that gives everyone a fair opportunity to compete and helps consumers make informed decisions.”

Although the case is still ongoing and has just begun, the results of the lawsuit could change how brokerages list their properties on MLS databases. The amended complaint argues that Compass “wants to have its cake and eat it too,” where the brokerage may benefit from listings provided by other brokerages onto each MLS, without having to add their own listings into the database.

Initially, ARMLS and its fellow organizations filed the lawsuit against Compass on Oct. 21, after California Regional Multiple Listing Service (CRMLS) filed its initial complaint against the brokerage a few weeks prior.

MLSListing’s participation in the lawsuit adds another name to Compass’s list of disgruntled MLSs. The New York-based MLS, OneKey® MLS, had also joined CRMLS as a plaintiff in its federal lawsuit against Compass last week.

Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years in prison

The affluential luxury real estate brokers, Tal and Oren Alexander, along with their brother Alon were sentenced to 30 years in federal prison last week.

Earlier in March, the brothers were found guilty on all charges of rape and sex-trafficking, after several named and unnamed women came forward and shared their stories.

One victim, under the pseudonym Isa Brooks, stated that she was just 16 years old when two of the brothers and their friend had raped her.

“I cry for the innocence of that terrified 16-year-old and stand for her today,” Brooks said, reported by CNN. “Their eyes went black. As if I was being mauled by animals.”

“I grieve the girl that I was,” she said.

The case began toward the end of 2024, where the brothers were arrested on charges of operating “a long-running sex trafficking scheme, as part of which they raped and sexually assaulted women to whom they had provided ‘material benefits,’ including domestic and international travel to vacation destinations, luxury accommodations at high-end hotels and vacation properties, and access to other luxury experiences and events,” according to a filed indictment.

Within the court proceedings, Judge Valerie Caproni showed little mercy for the brothers, who continued to claim their innocence to the charges throughout the sentencing process.

“Your crimes wreaked havoc on their lives. It has caused long lasting damage to them. Many have significant problems trusting people,” Caproni said, reported by CNN.

Despite several letters written to Caproni by friends and family of the Alexander brothers, Caproni once again reprimanded the trio for their crimes and their conduct.

“You did not have to stand up and say you’ve never raped anyone,” Caproni said, according to ABC News. “That’s a lie and you know it.”

Zillow pays out over $210 million to settle shareholders

After nearly five years of court proceedings, a settlement was reached in Jaeger v. Zillow Group litigation, in which shareholders argued that the portal did not adequately disclose its struggles to ramp up its now-defunct iBuying business, and misled investors.

Last Wednesday, Zillow announced that it would pay out over $212.5 million to the shareholders, who claimed that the portal had misrepresented the success of “Zillow Offers,” and failed to accurately disclose struggles it faced in flipping homes.

Both Zillow and Hagens Berman—the plaintiff’s attorneys for the case—have stated that they are satisfied with the settlement and await a judge’s approval.

“We are incredibly pleased to obtain this result for investors,” said Steve Berman, managing partner of Hagens Berman.

In a statement shared with RISMedia, a Zillow spokesperson commented, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

According to a regulatory filing from Zillow, about $48 million of the settlement will be paid through insurance proceeds. Hagens Berman said in a statement the settlement was “potentially the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington federal court.”

Prior to the settlement, the case was slated to reach trial in September 2027.

The case began with Zillow’s iBuying business, also known as Zillow Offers, which was launched in spring 2018. Zillow Offers was a house flipping initiative, where the company promised that it could scale the business model of buying and quickly flipping homes using technology to predict short-term market fluctuations and patterns.

Zillow Offers was shut down later in 2021, and sold a backlog of nearly 18,000 homes at a loss of about $550 million. Within the original complaint, Hagens Berman argued that several statements and communications from Zillow were “materially false and/or misleading” and had failed to disclose “material adverse facts” about Zillow’s business, operations and prospects.

Homebuyer sues Keller Williams over $650 “junk fee”

Broker fees are once again on the receiving end of litigation, as one homebuyer in Pennsylvania filed a complaint—consisting of over 30 pages—against Keller Williams Elite in Lancaster County’s Court of Common Pleas.

According to the complaint, Gregory Deivert, a recent buyer client, is suing the franchise over a $650 fee that he claims is essentially for nothing.

“The fee had no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it. It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for him,” the complaint states.

A final settlement statement was included in the filing, and the complaint references the breakdown of fees within the statement. Deivert’s attorney argues that the $650 broker fee is a prototypical “junk fee,” and that Keller Williams Elite was fully compensated for its services by the $14,700 commission it received from the seller.

The issue of “junk fees” is nothing new to the real estate industry. In 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) launched a formal inquiry into the issue of extra fees tacked onto home mortgage costs.

Generally, the complaint argues that customarily, broker fees are paid for by the seller and are included in the broker’s commission. Within the lawsuit, Deivert is suing the brokerage for a breach of fiduciary duty and a violation of the Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law.

As for relief, Deivert is asking for $50,000 from the brokerage, along with a declaration that Keller Williams Elite will be prohibited from charging the $650 fee again, and labeling it as a fixed fee for broker compensation without disclosing what it entails.
