#5638. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5637. Palantir beats Q3 forecasts as US commercial revenue overtakes government for first time

Shares of Palantir Technologies Inc. rose more than 1% in late trading today after the big-data analytics company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year revenue guidance for the third time this year.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Palantir reported adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents, up from 21 cents in the same quarter of last year, on revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 41 cents per share on revenue of $2.18 billion. It was the first quarter in which Palantir’s revenue topped $2 billion.

U.S. commercial revenue overtook U.S. government revenue for the first time in Palantir’s history. Sales to commercial customers in the U.S. reached $984 million, up 148% from a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Government sales rose 96%, to $953 million. Together they took total U.S. revenue to $1.937 billion, up 119% year-over-year.

Palantir closed 212 deals worth at least $1 million in the quarter, including 64 worth $10 million or more. Total contract value rose 6% from a year earlier, to $2.918 billion, after growing 151% in the same period of 2025. U.S. commercial remaining deal value climbed 79%, to $6.517 billion.

Net income more than doubled, to $1.128 billion from $476 million a year earlier, giving the company a 49% net margin. On an adjusted basis, operating income came to $1.427 billion at a 62% margin, and adjusted free cash flow was $1.216 billion. Palantir’s “Rule of 40” score hit 158%. The company ended September holding $10.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and U.S. Treasury securities.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Alex Karp used the earnings release to argue that what he called the “Sovereign AI movement” is creating “the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots” he has seen in 30 years in business. Governments and companies alike are being forced into one group or the other, “voluntarily or not,” according to Karp. That shift, he said, is “purpose-built for Palantir.”

Looking to the fourth quarter, Palantir expects revenue of $2.649 billion to $2.653 billion and adjusted operating income of $1.640 billion to $1.644 billion. Analysts had forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $2.46 billion.

Full-year revenue guidance now stands at $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion, up from the $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion Palantir forecast in August. U.S. commercial revenue is expected to exceed $3.559 billion, growth of at least 143%, and the company lifted its adjusted operating income outlook to a range of $5.245 billion to $5.249 billion. Adjusted free cash flow for 2026 is now forecast at $4.8 billion to $5 billion.

#5636. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5635. 10-Acre Florida Ranch With NBA-Level Facility Is Listed for $38.9 Million in Celebrity Enclave Where Gisele Bündchen Lives

An enormous 9.69-acre Florida compound with a brand-new 10,500-square-foot entertainment facility "that can be transformed into anything you can imagine" and resort-inspired grounds has just hit the market in Southwest Ranches for an astonishing $38.9 million.

If it reels in anywhere near its asking price, the 23,442-square-foot estate could become one of the top sales in the ultrahigh net worth neighborhood that celebrities, professional athletes, and supermodel Gisele Bündchen call home.

"I have never seen a property done to this scale before," says Tommy Crivello of the Tommy Crivello Real Estate Group, who is co-listing the property with Angeline Earnest of Coldwell Banker Realty.

Once the home of Mexican singer Juan Gabriel, the luxury residence last traded hands for $9,000,000 in 2022. Its asking price of $1,659 per square foot is currently the highest-priced listing in the exclusive Sunshine Ranches enclave of Southwest Ranches.

"Everything has been completely redone with extensive remodeling," Earnest notes. "The landscaping, garage, pools, and the 10,000-square-foot recreational facility are all new. Every structure also has a new roof."

The sprawling property boasts a five-bedroom primary residence, a three-bedroom guesthouse with a catering-grade kitchen, a members-style clubhouse with a full bar and private theater, and a gym and spa wellness retreat with a massage room and cold plunge.

Private lakes, immersive art, koi ponds, "producing orchards," a Tiki pavilion, and two pools, including one with a custom 10-foot rock-jumping wall, can also be found on the enormous lot. An outdoor basketball court and hockey rink round out the property.

"There are 10 acres of walkable space," she adds. "It feels like the whole property is livable and is not overwhelming."

"We are seeing a lot of high-end celebrities coming here," Crivello says. "I see an entrepreneur, hedge fund person, athlete, or real big car collector buying this property. It could also be someone who is looking for a place for the entire family, as it is designed for multigenerational living."

A custom-engineered lighting system transforms the pathways into nocturnal works of art. For equestrians, the sale also includes plans for a seven-stall barn with oversized paddocks.

"The property is large enough that there is room for another outdoor facility, and it has direct access to miles of riding trails," he says. "Everything in Southwest Ranches has rural zoning, so you can have a garden and any kind of animal on property. It just flows effortlessly."

Created as a "fully integrated private campus," the serene property also features art installations and curated gathering spaces for entertaining.

“You can get to the beach in 30 minutes, Amerant Bank Arena in 15 minutes, Las Olas Boulevard for the nightlife, and Pembroke Gardens is just 10 minutes away,” Crivello says. “You can retreat to the country, or you can be in the limelight as much as you want to be.”

Built in 1964, the Chicago brick-clad main estate boasts a renovated interior with two guest suites, each with a private entrance and that “function as private apartments within the residence.”

A lavish upstairs primary wing has a breakfast bar, a refrigerator, a seating area, dual bathrooms, separate closets, and a private terrace.

Other highlights include an executive office, a chef’s kitchen, a built-in wine preservation system, a custom bar, and a wraparound covered balcony on the main level.

A detached garage pavilion spanning nearly 2,000 square feet is fully air-conditioned. The four-vehicle structure has lift capability to accommodate up to eight vehicles. It also has floor drains, integrated compressor and vacuum systems, EV-ready outlets, workstation walls, and extra storage space.

One of the most impressive features of the property is its enormous entertainment facility, “currently home to a nonprofit basketball program.”

The “NBA-level” structure features professional athletic flooring, locker rooms, conference spaces, a viewing balcony, and a smoothie bar.

Its flexible design could also be reimagined into a 50- to 100-vehicle auto showroom, a private museum, a production studio, or an event venue.

“You could also transform it into an indoor equestrian facility. It offers the peace of mind that upscale riders want. #5634. 42AI launches with $62.5M to predict how traders act when markets turn volatile

Israeli artificial intelligence startup 42AI launched today with $62.5 million in funding to build what it calls a behavioral world model.

Its first customers are brokerages that want to know how individual traders will act when markets turn volatile. 42AI offers software that estimates the odds of each choice a person might make in a given situation. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch.

The company turns what it knows about a person into mathematical representations of personality traits, and a transformer-based world model works out the probabilities from there. A separate language model writes up which traits and context drove each prediction.

42AI says a brokerage can see what each client is likely to trade over the next 24 hours, including the instrument, the direction and the volume. If clients look set to pile into the same trade, a risk desk can hedge before the exposure lands on its book. Know-your-customer checks done at onboarding are one source of input, and the model also weighs how often a client calls and the sentiment in their voice.

Ten large brokerages are working with 42AI, which charges either a flat fee or a percentage of the value it helps generate. Revenue has reached seven figures, Gal-Or said, without giving a precise number.

By the company’s account, one brokerage gained about $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. The company also claims 98% accuracy on trades. That figure tracks whether trading flows land inside a predicted range, according to Gal-Or, and does not measure whether every individual trade was predicted correctly.

Three years of research went into the model. Thousands of people took psychological assessments in the first study, and by the time the team moved on to government and biobank datasets, the sample had passed 2 million. Customer data now spans about 30 million people.

Chief Technology Officer Ehud Ezra and three co-authors described one piece of the work in a paper posted in February. Their Large Behavioral Model adapts an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama 3.1 to predict a person’s strategic choices from a detailed psychometric profile.

Asked whether a brokerage could turn those predictions against its own clients, Ezra called it “a valid concern.” The founders pointed to regulation, monitoring and an internal ethics committee as checks on that kind of use.

Gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity are the next markets 42AI is exploring, with helping robots and AI agents understand people as a longer-term goal. Wherever it runs, the model loses accuracy when it misses outside influences, such as a trader acting on a colleague’s advice. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said.

The $62.5 million, which 42AI describes as seed funding, came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years. Amir Gal-Or, the startup’s co-founder and chairman, founded Infinity Group. Dan Shechtman, who won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is among the advisers to the research team. 42AI plans to raise more money.

#5633. Tribeca Dominates Manhattan Luxury Sales This Week With Top 2 Penthouses on Same Street

Tribeca took the crown for the hottest neighborhood in Manhattan luxury sales last week, nabbing the top two priciest sales in the borough.

The lower West Side neighborhood, which John F. Kennedy Jr. and his bride, Carolyn Bessette, did much to make famous, has continued to push toward the Hudson River with new luxury residential skyscapers.

Last week's top two sales were coincidentally on the same street, with contracts signed at 111 Murray St. and 71 Murray St. Both were penthouse condos.

"I like to call it 'Tribeca lite,'" says Brown Harris Stevens agent Lisa K. Lippman, who not only represents real estate in the neighborhood, but also lives in it. "It's not prime Tribeca."

The broker says "prime" Tribeca would be around the the area of Duane and North Moore Street. (JFK Jr. and Carolyn lived in 20 North Moore St.)

But as prime Tribeca filled up, development spread east and west—with the western edge closer to sweeping river views, as well as the Hudson River Greenway bike path and all of the riverfront parks and piers.

"The area feels less residential," she tells Realtor.com of Murray Street and the surrounding streets, which are packed with glass skyscrapers. "There's always people who want to be on a higher floor, have a lot of amenities, but pay a little less."

The top sale for the week ending Nov. 1 was Penthouse One at 111 Murray St., with an asking price of $33.95 million. The penthouse, inside a 64-story tower built in 2018 and designed by architect David Mann, was a sponsor sale.

The sprawling, extra-large unit—at 7,675 square feet with five bedrooms and 6.5 bedrooms—was snapped up by Richard Saghian, the founder and chief executive of Fashion Nova, for $31 million, according to multiple reports.

According to Forbes, the 45-year-old fashion mogul is worth $2.1 billion and is the No. 1,900–ranked richest person in the world.

The penthouse will be added to his growing property portfolio, which includes a $141 million Bel-Air mansion and two Miami Beach properties: a $30 million double lot and a $32 million estate.

His latest acquisition offers 360-degree views of New York Harbor, as well as 233 square feet of private terraces with which to enjoy them.

The sweeping river views really helped move the property, says listing agent Emily Sertic of Douglas Elliman, who has headed up sales in the building since its launch.

"You'll capture a glimpse of Central Park, the Empire State Building, all the historic bridges, the rivers, and the harbor," she says. "From its view line only, it really encompasses an incredible experience of New York. Everywhere you turn, there are these astonishing view lines that just go on and on."

"The view line and the grandeur of the space for entertaining was really important," she says of what helped attract the billionaire buyer, who was represented by Ryan and Emilia Serhant of Serhant.

The great room alone is over 2,000 square feet, says the broker, and boasts an eat-in kitchen, butler's pantry, and private terrace.

"Whether it's for work, entertainment, guests, or family, the bedrooms were a huge draw to the space," she says.

Saghian, the college dropout son of Iranian immigrants, is reportedly single with no children.

The fast-fashion mogul appears to appreciate a real estate deal—creditors of his Bel-Air mansion originally wanted $295 million at auction and a judge had to approve the sale because of the relatively low price it ended up fetching. And the Tribeca penthouse originally asked for $50 million back in September 2025.

"It has all the features that any trophy buyer is looking for," says Sertic.

Some of those features fit for a billionaire include a chef's kitchen with Wolf, Miele, and Sub-Zero appliances, dual fridges and dishwashers, a 60-inch custom gas cooktop, multiple ovens, and a full-height wine refrigerator.

The full-service luxury building contains the usual array of amenities one would expect at this price point.

There is a 24/7 door attendant, concierge service, and valet team; a full-service wellness center and spa complete with hammam, treatment rooms, and a 75-foot lap pool with private cabanas; a fitness center; a children's playroom with splash pad, and a teen arcade room. There's also a private dining room, screening room, and landscaped garden.

The penthouse comes with a $36,000 monthly fee, including HOA dues and taxes.

The second top sale of last week was also on Murray Street. The glass-walled triplex penthouse at 71 Murray St. is a four-bedroom, 4.5-bath unit with a price tag of $18.5 million.

Listed by Jeremy V. Stein of Sotheby's International Realty, the sprawling 6,700-square-foot condo included an astonishing 3,148-square feet of terraces, including two roof terraces decked out for entertaining with a full Viking kitchen, fire pit, and dining area. There is also a floating glass staircase and 36-foot climbing wall.

Topping a boutique building with only 12 residences, the penthouse has monthly common charges and taxes totaling $17,232.

The two downtown top sales aren't that unusual—the former warehouse district has been trendy since the late Kennedy scion took up residence there in the early 1990s. (Actor Robert DeNiro—who moved there in 1981—can truly claim pioneer status.)

Sertic says the typical neighborhood buyers tend to be "youngish buyers and their families" who work in the surrounding neighborhoods, especially the Financial District.

"A lot of our buyers walk to work," she says. "They are high-performing and fast-moving, so convenience is huge."

Despite Tribeca nabbing the top two sales, it was the Upper East Side that pulled the most luxury (over $4 million) contracts again this week. Of the 34 contracts signed, the UES dominated with the highest amount of sales for the 10th time this year.

As is usual, condos outsold co-ops, 17 to 12. However, with only five sales between them, co-ops are holding their own.

The upward sales trajectory of co-ops—where buyers tend to be subject to a rigorous board approval process—is likely the effect of luxury inventory being so slim, say experts.

It also probably helps that co-ops often trade lower than condos, with an average ask of $6.48 million versus $10.44 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty.

The most expensive co-op of the week was a new build, constructed in 2023. The Lenox Hill penthouse at 200 East 75th St. had an asking price of $16.85 million.

#5632. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5631. Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO

Anthropic PBC today published an updated version of the S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering.

The original document, which the company released last Monday, didn’t contain its third-quarter financial results. The new version reveals that Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue during the three months ended Sept. 30. That’s more than 11 times more than what it made a year earlier, but represents a deacceleration in quarter-over-quarter growth. Anthropic’s top line grew 47% on a quarterly basis, down from 144% three months earlier.

The artificial intelligence provider faces multipronged competition from open-source models, OpenAI Group PBC and tech giants such as Google LLC. The Alphabet Inc.’s newest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

Anthropic is investing heavily in training infrastructure to stay ahead of the competition. The company took a $5 billion charge in the third quarter because demand for computing hardware was higher than expected, which required it to purchase hardware at a premium. Hardware bought on short notice is more expensive than Anthropic’s usual capacity commitments, which it books 12 to 18 months before they’re needed.

The AI provider also took a $2 billion charge in connection with its non-cash employee donation matching program. That left Anthropic with a $536 million operating loss at the end of the third quarter. Three months earlier, it posted $974 million in operating income. Anthropic’s adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions, jumped by $300 million on a quarterly basis to $2.5 billion.

The company had $895.4 billion in outstanding infrastructure commitments as of Sept 30. Leases signed with Google LLC and Broadcom Inc. accounted for nearly a third of that sum. In April, the two companies agreed to supply Anthropic with several gigawatts of computing power powered by the search giant’s TPU chips, which Broadcom helped design. The AI provider also has computing deals with Amazon.com Inc., Oracle Corp. and SpaceX Technologies Corp. that are each worth more than $100 billion.

Anthropic plans to not only rent more computing capacity but also build its own data centers. The company’s purchase commitments jumped from $55 billion at the end of 2025 to about $314 billion in the third quarter.

Alongside the new financial figures, Anthropic’s revised S-1 filing provides an update about its efforts to mitigate AI risks. According to the document, the company is considering “to require human review and approval of certain” research tasks that are currently performed automatically by its models. It believes that its models will soon be capable of “dramatically” accelerating AI development.

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it plans to raise through its public offering. According to Bloomberg, the company hopes to at least match the $86.2 billion that SpaceX pulled in when it listed its shares earlier this year. Reuters reported that Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

#5630. Realtors Predict These Nine Cities Will Be Unaffordable by 2027

Vibrant-Colored neon lights on a busy night at the bars and honky-tonks in the country music center, Broadway, the tourism center of Downtown Nashville, Tennessee

(TNS)–Home prices are climbing across the nation and some markets are hotter than others. According to a new report from Finance Buzz, nine U.S. cities are likely to become unaffordable by 2027, due to an influx of out-of-town buyers and tight inventory.

Here’s a look at the popular locales where housing costs are outpacing local incomes, as per Finance Buzz’s reporting:

Many areas in northern New Jersey are popular for people relocating out of New York City.

According to Daniel Smith, team lead at Smith Realty Team, homes in Montclair are expected to stay in high demand and continue commanding higher home prices.

“Retirees and pre-retirees are also targeting these towns because of their vibrant downtowns, access to health care, and cultural amenities, which makes competition even stronger,” he said.

Nashville attracted numerous new residents during the pandemic years, offering a lively city experience alongside lower taxes and a more affordable cost of living.

While home prices have come down slightly over the past year, the median sale price is currently $464,983 and real estate experts don’t expect a reduction any time soon.

Realtor Carla Gericke, with Porcupine Real Estate, said that “no income tax, easy access to Boston, and that elusive small-town feel with real community bones” is causing Nashua’s popularity to spike.

“Nashua’s median home price has soared to the $500,000 to $550,000 range, and demand keeps outpacing supply,” she said.

Gericke urged retirees looking to buy in the state to act quickly or venture outside the bigger cities to find better deals.

Arizona has long been a top destination for retirees hoping to escape the cold. Fred Loguidice, a real estate expert and founder of several home-buying companies in the area, said that home demand is outpacing supply, making it a market that is likely to stay competitive in the future.

“In markets like Phoenix, fewer homes are being built while demand persists, so prices consistently escalate,” he said.

Real estate expert Fred Loguidice also highlighted demand for Northeast hubs like the Buffalo metro area. While Zillow put the median home price at a moderate $261,300, home values in the area have been increasing.

“That momentum is a hard habit to break,” he said, noting its affordability and surging job opportunities make it a top choice for relocation for people in the region and beyond.

Athens is about 60 miles northeast of Atlanta and attracts many buyers and visitors alike with its lively college town atmosphere, excellent dining scene, and more.

While Georgia is often cited as a top spot to retire, thanks to the weather and lower cost of living, real estate trends indicate that home prices will continue to climb throughout the next year or so. Prices have gone up over the past year, with the median currently sitting at $353,333.

Florida boasts many affordable cities and tax incentives for retirees, but those considering Tampa may want to reassess.

Omer Reiner, realtor and president of Florida Cash Home Buyers, said home prices in the city are already high, and rising insurance costs are putting many popular areas out of reach.

“This is especially true for those nearing or at retirement, as higher costs of living when you are on any type of fixed income means you are spending more for less,” he said.

Iowa isn’t particularly known for its excessive home prices, but demand has been on the rise in Des Moines, according to real estate investor Jacob Naig, particularly for homes popular with retirees.

“Single-family homes, as well as small multi-family properties and single-level ranch-style homes that are particularly desirable to aging buyers, have seen a substantial rise in demand,” he said.

Many cities in the Pacific Northwest have seen rapidly rising home prices, and Ontario, which sits on the border of Oregon and Idaho, is no different. With stunning desert views, mountain ranges, and more, it’s a haven for outdoorsy types.

But recent real estate trends indicated it could be unaffordable in the coming years. Average home prices have risen steadily over the past year and currently sit at $307,769.

#5629. 9 of the world's deepest lakes, from Crater Lake to Baikal

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Earth's 9 deepest lakes include one buried under Antarctic ice and a sea that counts as a lake. See how deep each one goes.

Stand at the edge of a lake whose floor no one can see, and the mind starts filling the dark water with stories. People have played this game for a long time. Myths from many parts of the world circle back to the bottomless lake, a body of water with no visible end below the surface. Storytellers have stocked those depths with monsters, drowned cities, hoards of treasure, mermaids, and the realms of the dead. Each image answers the same unease. Water hides what lies beneath it, and a basin with no apparent bottom hides everything.

Modern tools have stripped away much of the old guesswork. Sonar, remote cameras, and miniature submarines let scientists probe places that earlier generations left to fantasy. The mystery survives. A sounding turns a fabled abyss into a pit with a charted limit, yet a number on a map does little to quiet questions about what lives down there or what lurks out of reach. Hard data and stubborn imagination pull against each other in these places, and neither side has won. Exact numbers can show how far the descent runs. They cannot reveal what the lake has kept.

Britannica counts down the nine deepest lakes on Earth in a list that Noah Tesch wrote and the publication's editors fact-checked. The countdown opens with the shallowest of the nine and works toward the deepest, giving each entry's depth in feet with the metric equivalent alongside. Every entry pairs that figure with a short portrait touching on where the lake sits, how it formed, what inhabits it, how people use it, or what sets it apart. The list does not say how or when anyone took the readings. This article reports each figure as printed. The slides that follow keep the same order, from the ninth spot up to the first.

Crater Lake plunges 1,943 feet (592 meters) in the Cascade Range of southwestern Oregon, farther down than any other lake in the U.S. The basin is young by geologic measure. It formed about 7,700 years ago, after the giant volcano Mount Mazama erupted and collapsed. Water fills the space where the mountain stood. The country's record for depth, in other words, belongs to a basin that took shape while people lived in the region.

The Klamath may carry an echo of the disaster. Many believe the Klamath Indians' oral traditions about the lake's origins preserve a genuine memory of the event, wrapped in myth. Such traditions move by voice, from one generation of speakers to the next. Any memory of Mount Mazama's fall would have endured thousands of years of retelling on speech alone. If the belief holds, the Klamath account stands apart from the old tales that place monsters, drowned cities, and realms of the dead beneath bottomless waters. A real catastrophe sits at its core.

Crater Lake has no stream feeding it and no channel carrying water away. Precipitation, the rain and snow that land on the basin, provides its main supply. Without rivers, the lake receives nothing that streams would carry in from nearby slopes. The National Park Service credits the lake's deep blue color and clarity to water that contains almost nothing except water.

A single cataclysm explains most of the traits the lake shows today. Mount Mazama's destruction opened the basin, left a closed bowl filled from the sky, and may have given the Klamath a narrative worth passing on. The depth, the legend, and the blue water all trace back to one doomed peak in the Cascades. No other lake in the countdown has a creation story that many believe reflects its true and violent beginnings.

Great Slave Lake drops 2,015 feet (614 meters) in Canada's Northwest Territories, edging past the depth Crater Lake reaches in Oregon. Its name comes from an Athabascan-speaking group, the Slave or Slavey. The lake bears a people's name, yet few people live around it.

Two limbs, the North Arm and the East Arm, give the lake an irregular outline. The East Arm divides into two sections, with Christie Bay to the south and McLeod Bay to the north. The Slave River provides the main inflow, and the Mackenzie River drains the basin toward the Arctic Ocean. The river shares the Slave name, so one label marks both the basin and its chief source of water. Its outflow ends in a polar sea, the frozen north whose climate governs daily life here.

A punishing northern climate keeps people scarce along these shores. Yellowknife, the territory's biggest city, holds fewer than 20,000 residents. Every other town in the Northwest Territories has fewer people still. Yellowknife sits on the North Arm, which puts the territory's largest population center on the lake's own shoreline.

The same cold turns the frozen surface into a seasonal roadway. Britannica notes that the few residents hardy enough to stay enjoy certain perks, and the ice delivers one of them. Great Slave Lake freezes thick enough to bear cars and trucks for almost half the year. Each winter day, several hundred vehicles take an ice road that cuts the trip between Yellowknife and the community of Dettah. Traffic on that scale, in a territory with so few inhabitants, suggests the shortcut forms part of ordinary winter routine for many locals.

The shortcut disappears for the rest of the year, when the ice cannot hold that traffic. Travelers $TRV between Yellowknife and Dettah lose their route across the lake in those months. One climate both thins the population and builds the winter route its residents drive.

Lake Ysyk extends 2,192 feet (668 meters) down in Kyrgyzstan, and its surface stays open through winters in which temperatures fall to −15 °F (−26 °C) as a matter of routine. The Kyrgyz name for the lake, Ysyk-köl, translates as "Hot Lake," a title the unfrozen water earns each year.

Scientists credit the lake's slight salinity and geothermal activity in the surrounding area for keeping ice from forming. UNESCO points to low salinity and warm springs as well, and it adds the basin's depth to the list of causes. The same plunging basin that earns Lake Ysyk a spot in this countdown helps it hold off the cold. Depth cannot do the job alone, though. Great Slave Lake, the previous entry on the list, falls just short of Ysyk's measure, yet its ice hardens into a winter roadway. Ysyk's chemistry and the heat beneath it supply what its basin cannot.

The Scythians, the earliest settlers of Kyrgyzstan, left gold and bronze artifacts that have turned up near the lake, evidence of a long human presence on its shores. The lake also served as an important stop along the Silk Road. Medieval settlements lie in its shallows, remnants of periods when the water stood lower. The record stretches across eras, from the country's first settlers through the Silk Road years to medieval villages now under water.

The lake's buried history and great depth have drawn researchers and treasure hunters alike. The two groups chase the same waters for different prizes, one after knowledge and the other after riches. Expeditions set out from time to time in search of a "Kyrgyz Atlantis," ancient ruins that legend places in the lake's deeper reaches. The submerged medieval sites show the lake has risen over human communities at least once before. Their presence gives the Atlantis legend a real pattern to build on.

Lake Nyasa runs 2,316 feet (706 meters) to its floor and supports exceptional biodiversity across habitats that stand apart from one another. Three physical traits carve out those zones: the lake's length, its depth, and the layered temperatures of its water. Nyasa's outline is relatively long and narrow, so the basin stretches far in one direction while its water column stacks layer upon layer below the surface.

Each trait splits the lake along a different axis. Length spreads conditions out from one end to the other. Depth and temperature layering pile them from the surface down. Together they turn a single basin into a set of separate environments, and a creature suited to one stretch or layer meets very different conditions in the next.

Cichlids make up the great majority of the species living in those environments. One group of fish supplies most of the variety that sets Nyasa apart. Counting the lake's species comes close to counting its cichlids.

Nyasa's richness of life traces back to the shape and structure of its basin, and most of that richness swims as cichlids.

O'Higgins/San Martín Lake reaches 2,742 feet (836 meters) down, deeper than any of the four lakes before it in the countdown, yet Britannica judges it probably the least known lake on the list. Its basin lies in a stretch of the Patagonian Andes where few people live. The sparse population fits that obscurity.

The Argentina-Chile border runs across the water, and each country gives the lake its own name. Chileans call it O'Higgins. Argentines call it San Martín. The double title writes the border into the name itself. Readers meet the division before they learn anything else about the place.

Glacial meltwater enters from the west, where the O'Higgins Glacier reaches the lake. The glacier also sheds rock flour, stone ground to a fine powder, and the particles stay suspended in the water at high concentrations. Those particles turn the lake a milky turquoise.

The ice that tints the lake shares its name with the Chilean title for the water.

Lake Vostok holds water 2,950 feet (900 meters) deep beneath nearly 2.5 miles (4 km) of Antarctic ice, making it the largest known subglacial lake. Its frozen ceiling sets it apart from every other entry in the countdown. No boat crosses its surface, and no shoreline offers visitors a view. The ice overhead runs more than four times thicker than the water column below it. Of the full distance from the open air down to the lake floor, the water itself fills less than a fifth.

Confirming what the ice concealed took decades. Scientists suspected from the 1970s onward that a large body of fresh water sat trapped beneath the Antarctic sheet. British and Russian researchers produced exact measurements of the lake only in 1996. The long wait shows that the ice guarded even the basin's basic outline.

Mapping the basin left a larger question open. Nobody could collect water from the lake or install sensors under so much ice. Any biology in Vostok stayed a puzzle as a result. Knowing the lake's size told scientists nothing about whether anything lived in it, and settling the matter required a sample of the water itself.

A drilling team broke the impasse in 2012 by boring all the way down to the lake's surface. The breakthrough arrived 16 years after the exact measurements and more than 30 years after the first suspicions of a buried lake. Reaching the water posed a harder problem than sizing it. Scientists who examined the recovered samples report finding many new forms of bacterial life. Their account puts living organisms under a frozen lid that exceeds the depth of every lake in the countdown, Baikal included. If the samples bear that out, the ice that held drills at bay for so long never shut life out of the lake.

The Caspian Sea runs 3,360 feet (1,025 meters) deep, and only Lake Tanganyika and Lake Baikal sink farther on this list. Its name calls it a sea, yet Britannica counts it among the lakes and leaves the label unresolved. The question of what to call it does nothing to its depth, which earns it the third spot in the countdown.

The Caspian stretches between the Caucasus Mountains and the Central Asian Steppe. From north to south it covers nearly 750 miles (1,200 kilometers), and its average width comes to 200 miles (320 kilometers). The length works out to almost four times the width, giving the water the outline of a long corridor. A shape so drawn out leaves room for conditions at one end to bear little resemblance to those at the other.

The floor tilts toward the south. Across the northern third, the water averages about 20 feet (6 meters) deep. The southern third averages about 1,000 feet (300 meters), roughly 50 times the northern figure. Even that southern average falls short of the depth Crater Lake reaches at the shallow end of this countdown. The listed depth more than triples the southern average, so some part of the basin must drop far below the typical floor of either third. A single headline number hides a body of water that is shallow across one broad stretch and deep across another. The middle third goes without an average in the list, leaving the shape of the slope between the two extremes unknown.

Commercial fishing and shoreline tourism carry significant weight in the economies of the countries around the sea. A list built on depth says nothing about those industries. Much of the sea's value to its neighbors flows through its fish and its shores, two assets the 3,360-foot figure does not capture.

Lake Tanganyika runs 4,710 feet (1,436 meters) deep along a border shared by Zambia, Burundi, Tanzania, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its floor sits 1,350 feet below the Caspian Sea's, the widest gap between any two neighboring entries in the countdown. Only Lake Baikal outstrips it, by 605 feet.

Tanganyika shares its long, narrow profile with Lake Nyasa, and Britannica credits both with extraordinary biodiversity. The likeness ends at the surface. Tanganyika's basin reaches more than twice the depth of Nyasa's. Shape and species richness link the pair, while vertical scale divides them.

Shore communities have lived off Lake Tanganyika's fish since the Stone Age. Commercial methods reached the lake in the 1950s, and Britannica ties them to the overfishing of recent decades. A food source that sustained lakeside villages across thousands of years has come under strain within a single lifetime.

PIPELINE-SHORTFALL: Slide 8 — The source gives Lake Tanganyika only its depth, four bordering countries, a shared long and narrow shape and biodiversity with Lake Nyasa, Stone Age fishing, and 1950s commercial methods adding to overfishing. No approved web details cover the lake, so the slide runs about 145 words against the 300-word minimum. The editor cut a vague closing line and added no filler.

Vocabulary flag: 'lake' and 'deep/depth' recur from earlier paragraphs because no precise synonym exists.

Lake Baikal plunges 5,315 feet (1,620 meters), farther than any other lake in the countdown. It outstrips Lake Tanganyika, its nearest rival, by 605 feet (184 meters), a margin wide enough that the final spot never looks contested.

Baikal reaches more than 2.7 times as far down as Crater Lake, the opening entry on the list. A full 3,372 feet (1,028 meters) separate the floors of the two basins. Crater Lake holds the U.S. record, yet it could sink into Baikal and leave more than half of Baikal's drop still below it.

Baikal's living inventory sets it apart as sharply as its sheer descent. Many of its plants and animals exist nowhere else on Earth. Other entries on the list share that trait. Homegrown species run through the countdown as a pattern, and Baikal supplies one of its strangest examples.

The Baikal seal, also called the nerpa, stands out among the most striking of those residents. No other seal species lives in fresh water alone. Every other kind of seal spends at least part of its existence outside fresh water. The nerpa is an outlier within its own family.

The nerpa's arrival remains a puzzle. Baikal sits hundreds of miles inland, and nobody knows how the seal's ancestors got there. The distance from any coast sharpens the riddle. An animal whose relatives all use waters beyond the freshwater world somehow took hold deep in the interior of a continent. Baikal closes the countdown with a resident everyone can name and nobody can account for.

VOCABULARY FLAG: The roots 'lake' (paragraphs 1 and 3 context) and 'deep' (paragraph 5) recur and have no precise synonym in this context.

#5628. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5627. Rack-scale AI: How Dell and AMD are building infrastructure

Dell Technologies Inc. and its partner Advanced Micro Devices Inc. face similar competitive pressures. Both tech powerhouses operate in a business climate where success is now measured across central processing units, graphics processing units, rack-scale systems, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar.

The pressure to compete across those measures underscores what theCUBE Research has termed “Engineering Velocity.” Since the Dell Technologies World event in May, AMD and Dell have not slowed their pace of collaborations and announcements.

AMD and Dell are working to build enterprise AI infrastructure that can keep pace with changing workloads and customer requirements.

“In AI infrastructure, the winner may not be the company with the best benchmark on keynote day,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “It will more likely be the company whose engineering system learns, validates and improves the entire platform faster than anyone else.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale” and its past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

A cornerstone of the Dell and AMD relationship is the server giant’s PowerEdge portfolio. Dell expanded its PowerEdge server line in May and has followed that up with additional details surrounding the integration of AMD processors.

The two companies have pursued a strategy designed to facilitate server consolidation as agentic AI drives a surge in demand for general-purpose compute. Agents rely heavily on CPUs, yet data centers don’t have a lot of extra room to add servers in rooms already stacked with GPUs.

Systems powered by AMD processors will deliver 70% gen-over-gen performance gains and can fold 13 servers from Dell’s 14th PowerEdge generation into one, according to Pradyumna Narendra, product planner and senior consultant at Dell.

“For every 10 to 13 servers you replace, you get so much of that productivity gain back because now you can do that with one server,” he told theCUBE. “When you expand that across data centers, that’s like an accelerating effect that you get to capitalize from.”

Dell and AMD must also accommodate a wealth of AI use cases and the accompanying demand for compute. Dell’s three-rack-unit server requires less power for cooling than a two-unit equivalent, allowing customers to pack more computing power into each rack, according to Narendra.

“By deploying servers that are slightly larger in package, you deliver more density at a rack level, which seems sometimes counterintuitive,” he explained. “As AI accelerates, inferencing and agentic AI around it will accelerate and grow faster. As these use cases scale out, you get exponential growth in the need for compute.”

Beyond server consolidation, Dell and AMD have been steadily enhancing a modular solution to simplify AI deployment and scaling: the Dell AI Platform with AMD.

The on-premises enterprise AI solution integrates AMD Instinct accelerators and EPYC processors with Dell PowerEdge servers, PowerSwitch networking and PowerScale storage for model training, fine-tuning and high-throughput inference. The platform is designed to let customers begin with configurations that meet current workloads and expand compute and GPU density over time, without rearchitecting.

“What we’re finding is customers want modular solutions. They want to think about [solutions] across the whole platform,” said Varun Chhabra, senior vice president of product marketing and infrastructure solutions group at Dell, in a discussion with theCUBE. “Compute, storage, networking [and] GPU. The software framework on top of it, the models: Have they all been tested? Have they all been validated?”

Dell has integrated the AMD ROCm software stack into the platform to support training, fine-tuning and serving large language models on-premises. The modular platform lets customers begin with smaller deployments and expand on the same infrastructure, according to Chhabra.

“You can start small with these composable units of storage, compute, networking, pre-integrated with AMD Instinct and EPYC CPUs with the ROCm software as well as the open ecosystem that sits on top of it,” he said. “We test it, we validate it, and the customers can use it and once they start seeing value in it, they know they can scale in a modular way with the same frameworks.”

Dell announced support for AMD Instinct MI350P PCI Express GPUs in its PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers beginning in July, giving enterprises another option for scaling agentic and generative AI deployments. It also represents an important boost in memory bandwidth which matters in time-to-first-token latency.

The MI350P offers 144 gigabytes of HBM3E memory, which can be a key differentiator for inference performance, according to Mike Darby, senior manager of business development, Instinct Data Center GPUs, at AMD, during an appearance on theCUBE.

“It’s a lot of memory, but it’s also HBM3E, so [it has] an amazing amount of bandwidth,” he said. “The main use case being inference: It’s all about that latency, time to first token [and] the user experience, so that your attention span doesn’t move somewhere else while you’re waiting for your response.”

AMD and Dell’s collaboration on PCIe integration has another angle worth watching. AMD’s PCIe-based GPU supports air-cooled deployments, providing users with a path to deploy AI within existing data center infrastructure.

As the tech industry has encountered resistance in recent months to the buildout of large data centers across the U.S., concerns have centered on the environmental impact and use of water-based cooling systems. Separately, Dell found that, as it deployed its next-generation PowerEdge servers, some enterprise customers were still not prepared to adopt liquid cooling within data centers.

“Working with Dell, we added a PCI card to our air-coolable roadmap for GPU Instinct so that it fit in more Dell PowerEdge servers that go to the broader enterprise,” said Robert Hormuth, corporate vice president of architecture and strategy for the Data Center Solutions Group at AMD, during a conversation with theCUBE. “Not everybody is adopting direct liquid cooling.”

Dell’s work with AMD this year has extended beyond joint product announcements. In June, the two companies announced a partnership with the University of Cambridge to establish a Sovereign AI Innovation Lab (SAIL) in the United Kingdom.

The collaboration is designed to help advance the next generation of AI infrastructure and AI-powered scientific breakthroughs. It builds on Cambridge’s expanded AI research infrastructure, including the Zenith AI supercomputer, powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators integrated into Dell infrastructure.

Dell and AMD have also collaborated in recent months on a telecom initiative with AT&T Inc. Telecom data is a heavy lift when it comes to AI, with AT&T having processed over one trillion tokens to train models. AMD has provided the high-performance hardware foundation for both training and inference workloads involving the OTel 2.0 models developed through the Open Telco AI initiative.

Dell integrated this technology with AI-optimized servers for telecom environments to create a production-grade foundation for operators across data-intensive, real-world network environments. OTel 2.0’s training infrastructure uses Dell’s PowerEdge XE9785 server configured with eight MI355X GPUs.

The alliance between Dell and AMD highlights a key development in the growing AI infrastructure market: There are plenty of opportunities for competition. Both Dell and AMD appear committed to building portfolios that offer enterprise choices in AI processing solutions.

“AMD didn’t present its new products … as ‘respectable alternatives,’” Vellante said. “It claimed outright leadership across CPUs, GPUs, rack-scale performance, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar. It extended the argument across enterprise AI, robotics, ultra-low-latency inference and a rapidly expanding partner ecosystem.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5626. Justin Baldoni Discreetly Sells Former Los Angeles Home for $2.1 Million After Making a ‘Fresh Start’ in Nashville

Actor Justin Baldoni discreetly offloaded his former Los Angeles home months after relocating to Nashville, TN, for a “fresh start.”

The three-bedroom, three-bathroom Culver City abode went for $2.1 million in an off-market transaction in August, according to Page Six. The 1,992-square-foot house was built in 1952 and sits on a 5,736-square-foot lot.

“He hasn’t lived there in years,” a People magazine source said. “The family has been living in Nashville for a bit now, but they moved to Ojai before that.”

The “It Ends With Us” director and his wife, Emily Baldoni, reportedly bought the home in 2017.

In an October 2020 People magazine interview, the couple opened up about life in the “urban farmhouse.”

The Baldonis said they invited loved ones to visit the home to write prayers and affirmations on its exposed wooden beams after completing a nine-month renovation.

“In the beams of the house is literally love,” Justin said.

The home had a host of interesting features, including a climbing wall in the garage for their children, Maiya and Maxwell.

There was also a built-in Wolf coffee machine and a top-of-the line Kohler toilet the actor compared to a “Transformer.”

While Emily shared that the plumbing feature “takes care of everything,” Justin noted that the family “didn’t panic as much as some others when all the toilet paper disappeared.”

The sale of the Los Angeles property isn’t the only quiet real estate move Justin, 42, has made this year.

Property records indicate that he listed his sprawling Ojai, CA, compound for $8.88 million on Feb. 5. The listing came just days after a rental listing for the same property—which was asking $40,000 a month—was taken down.

The estate, which the couple purchased for $2.2 million in 2020, has since been taken off the market.

The five-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom dwelling on a 10-acre lot in the picturesque neighborhood of Santa Paula was described by Emily as a “magical place” in a 2023 Architectural Digest interview.

Inspired by their trips abroad, the couple went to lengths to design “the whole house with feng shui in mind,” a practice inspired by his mother, “who’s done it for 30 years.”

“When we went to Tulum and parts of Mexico, we would take pictures of lamps or couches—just as inspiration—and then we started to put together a Pinterest board of things that we liked,” he said.

The couple made a series of upgrades to the home to create a “sanctuary.” According to the since-removed listing, the home was outfitted with “a state-of-the-art medical-grade air filtration system,” electromagnetic frequency shielding around the primary bedroom, a saltwater pool, and a “regenerative orchard.”

It also included a hot tub, sport court, custom-designed gym, LED-lit in-ground trampoline, koi pond with waterfall, fire pit, and walking paths.

Additional technological amenities included EV charging stations, a state-of-the-art security system, and fire mitigation systems.

The family packed their bags for Tennessee in December 2025, amid the highly publicized legal drama Justin was involved in after actress Blake Lively sued in 2024, claiming he had sexually harassed her during the filming of “It Ends with Us.”

“It’s obviously been an incredibly difficult time for the whole family, but Nashville has given them a fresh start,” a People magazine source previously shared.

After denying the allegations, Justin filed a $400 million countersuit against Lively and her husband, Ryan Reynolds, her publicist Leslie Sloane, and Sloane’s PR firm, citing defamation and breach of contract.

The suit was later dismissed by a judge, as were Lively’s sexual harassment claims. The actress later pursued allegations of retaliation against Justin, as well as his production company and publicity team.

Justin and Lively reached a private settlement days before the case was due to go to trial in May 2026.

However, the dispute continued when Lively sought $8 million in legal fees from Justin. She was awarded a total of $407,451.75 in an Aug. 26 order.

In July, when the dispute was still ongoing, the Baldonis posted an Instagram Reel to address the situation for the first time.

“We have not spoken publicly for the better part of the last two years, and it’s not because we haven’t had anything to say,” Justin said. “It just felt like every time we went to make a video like this, we wanted to speak, something was telling us not to. It just didn’t feel like the right time, and we were talking about it and feeling into it and praying about it.”

While Justin kept his statement fairly vague and never named Lively, the couple did share that they had experienced a lot of “trauma.”

"What I will say is that there have been so many painful things that have been spoken into existence over the last couple of years,” he said. “That created so much noise, and we didn’t want to add to the noise. So we just wanted to let the justice system run its course."

The couple noted that they had “so much more to say,” but that they were “going to focus on continuing the healing” and “hanging out” with their “kiddos and enjoying life.”

According to the New York Post, the family’s new Nashville home is a $3.4 million newly built abode. The six-bedroom, six-bathroom property spans 7,000 square feet and is situated on an acre lot.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.
