#5625. Exit polls are surveys, not vote counts: how they work and where they strain

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How exit polls work, from precinct sampling to reweighting, and what notable elections in the U.S., U.K. and Ukraine show about their limits

The first numbers that appear on an election-night broadcast usually come from a survey, not a count. They reflect what a sample of voters told interviewers on the way out of their polling places. That survey is built to be corrected as real returns arrive. Understanding how exit polls work explains why the early picture can shift before the night is over.

Exit polls do two separate jobs. The first is to help news organizations project winners once polls close. The second is to explain the result: who voted for which candidate, how age, race and education lined up with those choices, and what views voters brought with them. The demographic tables that networks publish after an election come from this second job.

The method has limits. Pollsters interview voters at a sample of precincts rather than at every polling place. Early and mail voters never walk past an interviewer, so pollsters reach them by telephone. Some voters decline to take part. If one candidate's supporters refuse more often than the other's, the raw numbers lean the wrong way. Figures that leak during the afternoon are unweighted, raw survey results. They have not yet been adjusted to match counted votes. That is why they can differ from the breakdowns published late at night or the next day.

Those limits have surfaced in public more than once. In the U.S., networks called Florida twice in 2000 and withdrew both calls. In 2002, the consortium that supplied exit poll data to the networks failed on election night, and its members later disbanded it. In 2004, leaked numbers pointed toward John Kerry in key states before George W. Bush won. In the U.K., the 1992 exit poll pointed to a hung parliament before John Major's Conservatives won a majority.

Not every case is a story of bad data. In 1980, the controversy centered on when NBC projected the winner, not on whether its numbers were right. In Ukraine in 2004, exit polls were cited as evidence that the official count was wrong.

The first four slides cover the mechanics: what an exit poll is, how precincts and voters are chosen, where the method came from and why the numbers move. The other six examine elections in the U.S., U.K. and Ukraine where projections, data or systems went wrong or collided with official results.

An exit poll is a survey of voters taken on election day, mostly as people walk out of their polling places. Respondents say how they voted and answer questions about their age, race, education and views on the issues.

That pairing of choice and profile sets an exit poll apart from the vote count. Official tallies, which election officials compile and certify, record how many ballots each candidate received. They say nothing about who cast those ballots. An exit poll fills that gap by linking each answer to a voter's characteristics.

In the U.S., Edison Research runs the exit poll for the National Election Pool. The pool is a group of news organizations that share a single survey instead of each commissioning its own. Its members include ABC, CBS, CNN and NBC.

Not every major outlet is still in the pool. Fox News and the Associated Press stopped using the National Election Pool's exit poll. Both now rely on AP VoteCast, a separate survey run by NORC at the University of Chicago.

The two products reach voters on different schedules. The Edison exit poll centers on election day, with interviewers stationed outside polling places. AP VoteCast draws on interviews with voters both before and on election day. Its sample is not confined to people interviewed at a polling place on the final day.

The split matters for anyone switching channels on election night. A breakdown of how younger voters or college graduates voted on CNN or NBC comes from the Edison survey. A similar breakdown on Fox News or in an AP story comes from AP VoteCast. The two are separate surveys with separate methods. Their estimates for the same group of voters can differ.

Comparing figures across outlets starts with a basic check: which survey produced them. Neither survey replaces the official count, which remains the final record of who won.

Exit pollsters do not station interviewers at every polling place. They pick a sample of precincts designed to represent a whole state. Interviewers at those sites then approach departing voters at a fixed interval and hand them a short paper questionnaire.

The precinct is the first layer of the sample. A large state can have thousands of polling places, and staffing all of them on a single day is not practical. Pollsters instead choose a smaller set intended to reflect the state's electorate as a whole. The quality of the final estimate depends on how closely that set of precincts mirrors the state.

The individual voter is the second layer. At each sampled precinct, the interviewer does not simply approach whoever looks willing to talk. The interviewer follows a set interval instead, such as every third or fifth person to walk out. A fixed rule keeps the interviewer's own judgment out of the selection. Without it, a survey could tilt toward people who seem friendly, unhurried or similar to the interviewer.

Voters who agree to take part receive the questionnaire. It asks whom they voted for. It also covers their age, race and education, along with their views on the issues in the race. The respondent fills in the form rather than answering out loud. No one has to announce a choice to a stranger outside a polling place.

In-person interviews miss a sizable group of voters: people who cast ballots early or by mail. Those voters never walk out of a precinct on election day. An interviewer at the door has no way to reach them. Pollsters add telephone interviews to capture that group. The phone results are combined with the in-person questionnaires to describe the full electorate.

The method's central weakness is non-response. Some voters who are approached decline to take part. Refusals alone do not ruin a survey. The problem arises when one candidate's supporters say no more often than the other candidate's supporters. In that case, the completed questionnaires overrepresent one side. The raw result then skews toward the side that answered more readily, even if every precinct in the sample was well chosen.

Warren Mitofsky, a statistician at CBS News, is credited with developing the exit poll. CBS used the method in the 1967 race for governor of Kentucky, the starting point for a survey format U.S. networks still rely on.

Before joining CBS, Mitofsky worked at the U.S. Census Bureau. The federal agency runs the national census and a wide range of household surveys.

The exit poll changed the question pollsters asked. A pre-election survey asks people how they plan to vote, and some of them never turn out. An exit poll asks people who have just voted what they did. That gives a news organization a read on actual voters rather than likely ones, before any official tally is released.

Mitofsky did not stop at the survey itself. He built the exit poll into the system the networks used to project winners on election night. Those projections let anchors call a race on air without waiting for every ballot to be counted. The same data also gave reporters a way to describe which groups of voters backed each candidate.

His work in polling reached beyond election day. With Joseph Waksberg, a Census Bureau statistician, he developed the Mitofsky-Waksberg method. It is a technique for drawing random samples of telephone numbers. Random-digit dialing of this kind became a widely used approach for telephone surveys. Mitofsky also helped create the CBS News/New York Times poll, a long-running partnership between the network and the newspaper.

Decades after Kentucky, his name returned to the national exit poll. After Voter News Service collapsed in 2003, Edison/Mitofsky took over the U.S. exit poll for the networks. The operation paired Edison Research with Mitofsky International, the firm Mitofsky ran. Its system for the National Election Pool was first used in the 2004 presidential election.

Mitofsky died in 2006. The exit poll format he introduced in Kentucky remains part of how U.S. networks cover election night.

Exit poll figures shift over election night because the first numbers are raw survey answers, and pollsters later reweight them to match actual vote counts. The breakdowns posted late at night or the next day are adjusted figures, not the same data that circulated in the afternoon.

Unweighted numbers come straight from the questionnaires collected so far. They reflect only the voters interviewed up to that point in the day. Morning voters can differ from those who vote after work. A partial day of interviews may not resemble the full electorate.

The adjustment begins once real returns come in. As precincts report, pollsters compare the survey's estimate of each candidate's share with the counted vote. If the survey shows a candidate doing better than the tally, the responses are reweighted so the poll's topline matches the count. The answers about age, race, education and views move along with that adjustment.

That step changes the demographic picture too. If one candidate's share in the poll drops to match the count, the groups that favored that candidate look different in the published tables. The estimate of how a particular group voted can move between an afternoon leak and the final release.

This is why leaked afternoon numbers are an unreliable guide to the outcome. Those figures have not yet been checked against a single counted ballot.

Exit polls serve two separate purposes, and reweighting matters most for the second. On election night, the survey helps decision desks project winners, often alongside early returns from sample precincts. Once votes are tallied, the same survey becomes a central record of who voted for whom and why.

The weighted version is the one that lasts. Analysts and journalists draw on it in the weeks after an election to describe each candidate's coalition and voters' priorities. Matching the survey to the result keeps that description consistent with how the electorate actually voted. Without the adjustment, it would reflect only the people who agreed to fill out a questionnaire.

On election night in 1980, NBC projected that Ronald Reagan had defeated Jimmy Carter while polls were still open in western states. Carter conceded before voting had ended on the West Coast.

The accuracy of NBC's call was never the issue. The exit poll data behind it pointed to the correct winner. NBC was then one of the three major U.S. broadcast networks, alongside ABC and CBS. Reagan, the Republican challenger, unseated Carter, the sitting Democratic president. The final Electoral College tally was 489 votes for Reagan and 49 for Carter.

The criticism focused on when the call reached viewers. A national election in the U.S. spans several time zones. Polling places in the East close hours before those in the Pacific states. A projection broadcast after eastern polls close can reach voters in California, Oregon and Washington state while they still have time to cast a ballot.

Carter's concession added to the timing problem. The sitting president had publicly accepted defeat. Western voters who had not yet gone to the polls heard from the candidate himself that the presidential race was over.

The episode fed a long-running debate over whether early projections discourage people from voting. The concern is that a voter who believes the top race is settled may stay home. Staying home also means skipping contests further down the ballot, such as races for Congress, state offices and local measures.

The debate turned on a question an exit poll cannot answer. A survey of voters leaving polling places can indicate who is winning. It cannot measure how many people skip voting because they heard a result on television.

The 1980 case differs from exit poll controversies in which the data went wrong. The numbers did not overstate a candidate, the system did not fail, and NBC did not have to retract its call. The issue was the gap between knowing a result and broadcasting it while part of the electorate was still voting.

On election night in 2000, the major U.S. television networks projected Florida for Al Gore and later took the call back. In the early morning, they projected the state for George W. Bush and retracted that call too.

The first projection rested partly on exit poll results and partly on returns from a sample of precincts. Those numbers pointed toward Gore. The networks made the call before polls had closed in the western Panhandle. That part of Florida sits in the Central time zone, while most of the state runs on Eastern time. Some Florida voters could still cast ballots after the state had already been projected.

As actual vote counts arrived, they no longer supported a Gore win. The networks withdrew the projection and returned Florida to the undecided column. With the rest of the map largely settled, the presidency now depended on that one state.

Florida carried 25 electoral votes in 2000. When the networks called the state for Bush in the early morning, they were in effect calling the election. Gore phoned Bush to concede. He then called back to withdraw the concession as the gap between the two candidates narrowed. The networks retracted their Bush projection as well.

The state was decided by a margin of a few hundred votes. The result came only after a recount and a ruling from the U.S. Supreme Court. In Bush v. Gore, decided on Dec. 12, 2000, the court halted the recount. Bush carried Florida and won the presidency, although Gore won the national popular vote.

The episode exposed two separate weaknesses. One was statistical. An exit poll is a sample survey. No sample survey can reliably separate two candidates in a contest decided by a few hundred votes out of millions cast. The other was timing. Projecting a state while some of its polling places remain open raises questions about whether the call affects who turns out.

Network executives were called to testify before a House committee in early 2001 about their election-night projections. Florida in 2000 showed that a projection is a judgment built on survey data and partial returns, not a final count.

Voter News Service, the shared exit poll operation of the major U.S. television networks and the Associated Press, failed on election night in November 2002. Its system did not deliver the usual exit poll data and vote results to its members, who disbanded it in January 2003.

The consortium rested on a simple idea. Instead of each network paying for its own nationwide survey, the members shared one exit poll and one stream of vote results. Voter News Service had supplied that exit poll data since 1990, through presidential and midterm elections alike.

That arrangement made every member dependent on a single supplier. A failure at Voter News Service would affect all of them at once, not just one network.

That is what happened in the 2002 midterm elections. On election night, the exit poll figures and vote results the members expected did not arrive in the usual way. The pooled design meant the gap reached every member newsroom at the same moment.

The 2002 episode was a failure of delivery. It was not a case of a poll arriving on time and leaning toward the wrong candidate. The members did not receive the data and results they had built their election-night coverage around.

Its members ended the arrangement rather than carry Voter News Service into another election cycle.

A replacement was ready in time for the next presidential election. Edison/Mitofsky built a new exit poll system for the National Election Pool, the group of news organizations that took over the shared survey. That system was first used in 2004, the year George W. Bush faced John Kerry.

The new setup kept the pooled approach but changed who ran the survey. The networks still shared one exit poll. Edison/Mitofsky, an outside research firm, now carried out the work for them.

The 2002 failure showed that an exit poll depends on infrastructure as well as method. Its numbers are of use to a newsroom only if they arrive on election night.

The 2004 U.S. exit poll overstated support for Democratic nominee John Kerry, and early numbers that leaked online made him look like the leader in key states. George W. Bush, the Republican incumbent, won a second term instead.

The leaked figures were raw, unweighted survey results. They had not yet been adjusted against any counted votes. Read at face value, they pointed toward a Kerry victory.

The final count went the other way. Bush won 286 electoral votes to Kerry's 251. One elector cast a ballot for John Edwards, Kerry's running mate and a senator from North Carolina. A candidate needed 270 electoral votes to win.

Ohio, with 20 electoral votes, decided the outcome. Without it, Bush would have fallen short of 270. Kerry conceded the day after the election.

The poll was conducted by Edison/Mitofsky for the National Election Pool, the group of news organizations that sponsors the U.S. exit poll. It was the first presidential election for the system Edison/Mitofsky built after Voter News Service was disbanded in 2003. That made 2004 an early public test of the new system.

In January 2005, Edison/Mitofsky released an evaluation of its election-day survey. The report found that the exit poll had overstated Kerry's support. Its explanation turned on who agreed to respond. Kerry voters, the report concluded, had been more willing than Bush voters to complete the questionnaire.

The pattern is known as differential non-response. An exit poll records only the answers of people who agree to take part. When one candidate's backers turn interviewers down more often, that candidate looks weaker in the survey than at the ballot box. In 2004, that meant the raw data understated Bush and inflated Kerry.

The same survey also supplied the demographic breakdowns of the 2004 electorate. They were reweighted to match the final results once the votes were counted.

The broadcast exit poll for the 1992 U.K. general election pointed to a hung parliament, with no party holding a majority in the House of Commons. The actual result gave John Major's Conservatives an overall majority of 21 seats.

The BBC and ITV commissioned the poll for their coverage of the vote on April 9, 1992. Its projection suggested that neither the Conservatives nor Neil Kinnock's Labour Party would be able to govern alone. A hung parliament would have meant talks over a coalition or a minority government.

That outcome never arrived. The Conservatives returned to power for a fourth consecutive term, and Major stayed in Downing Street. Kinnock resigned as Labour leader after the defeat.

The exit poll was not the only survey to miss. Most pre-election opinion polls had shown Labour level with the Conservatives or slightly ahead. The gap between the surveys and the count popularized the phrase "shy Tory." The label describes Conservative voters thought to be less willing to tell pollsters how they planned to vote or had voted.

Seat projections in Britain depend on vote shares in marginal constituencies, where small shifts decide which party wins. A modest underestimate of one party's support can turn a projected hung parliament into a working majority. In 1992 the projection understated the Conservatives.

Later British exit polls performed better. The 2015 and 2017 exit polls came much closer to the final results than the 1992 poll did. Since 2010 the exit poll has been a joint project of the BBC, ITV and Sky News.

The 2017 exit poll stood apart from the pre-election surveys. Theresa May called an early election that year, and many pre-election polls pointed to a Conservative majority. The exit poll released as voting ended signaled a hung parliament instead. The count produced exactly that. The Conservatives remained the largest party but lost their majority. May then formed a government with the backing of Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist Party.

In Ukraine's November 2004 presidential runoff, exit polls showed opposition leader Viktor Yushchenko in the lead. The official count declared Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovych the winner instead. That clash helped set off mass protests. A court-ordered rerun later gave Yushchenko the presidency.

The runoff pitted the two leading candidates against each other after neither won outright in the first round. Yanukovych was the sitting prime minister and had the backing of outgoing President Leonid Kuchma. Yushchenko, a former prime minister, led the opposition.

Yushchenko's supporters pointed to the exit polls as evidence that the official count did not reflect how people had voted. Large crowds gathered in Kyiv, centered on Independence Square $SQ. The demonstrations became known as the Orange Revolution, after the color of Yushchenko's campaign.

The dispute moved to the courts. Ukraine's Supreme Court threw out the runoff result and ordered the vote held again. The repeat runoff took place on Dec. 26, 2004, and Yushchenko won it. He took office as president in January 2005.

This case runs in the opposite direction from many well-known exit poll controversies. In the 2004 U.S. presidential election and the 1992 U.K. general election, the official count served as the benchmark, and the exit poll was the number that missed. In Ukraine, the exit poll was cited as the check on the official count.

The two measures capture different things. An exit poll records what a sample of voters say they did after leaving the polling station. An official count records the ballots that election authorities tally and report. Either one can go wrong. A survey rests on a sample, and a sample can miss. A count can go wrong through error or manipulation in how ballots are recorded and reported.

A gap between the two is a signal to investigate, not proof of which number is correct. In Ukraine, the rerun produced a result that matched the direction the exit polls had shown, not the original official tally.

#5624. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5623. Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem

For buyers, especially first-time buyers, today’s housing affordability crisis (driven by a host of market challenges, from rising mortgage rates to low inventory and lingering inflation) creates many barriers to entry for homeownership. Is there anything agents can actually do at the local level to move the needle and help their clients achieve their homeownership goals?

Four brokerage leaders recently gathered at RISMedia 38th Annual CEO & Leadership Exchange on a panel titled, “Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem,” to say yes and share their tactics and long-term solutions for buyers facing today’s housing affordability problem.

The session, moderated by RISMedia Founder and CEO John Featherston, included panelists Keith Smith, co-owner, Yes Realty Partners, a Keller Williams Alliance Partner; Ennis Antoine, owner and CEO, EA Realty of Georgia; Katey McGrath, vice president, director of operations, Elfant Wissahickon Realtors®; and Ken Baris, CEO, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Jordan Baris Realty.

Here’s a glimpse into some of the questions and answers that provided attendees with some detailed takeaways to help their clients overcome the affordability challenge.

John Featherston: To set the stage, tell us why brokers should care about the housing affordability issue?

Keith Smith: I’m just going to kind of say the awkward thing to the room. Every single one of us makes a living either directly or indirectly from helping people buy and sell. And if we can’t help people buy and sell, we’re not going to be able to put our key in the door. We’re not going to be able to begin our business. Right now, first-time homebuyers can’t buy, and they’re 40? You have Boomers who will not be able to move on. So if we can’t help people do that, this isn’t just a certain entry point. It’s all the way across the board. I think maybe a little bit later we’ll talk about some possible solutions.

Katey McGrath: Obviously it’s good business. And what’s interesting too is at least in our market, the competition for that business is a lot less intense because it is a little bit more work and it’s not as dollar-productive. It’s absolutely more rewarding and more valuable to your communities, but not everybody gets up and says, “I want to sell lower-priced houses.” And so I love new agents getting into the business and focusing on affordability. We love training them up to pre-qualify renters because most of the time the renters don’t know they can buy a house. So it’s a great way to start your real estate business.

And in our company, we have a lot of things that sort of reinforce that culture of homeownership as the most impactful thing you can do in a community. We also create programs in-house that help leverage gift funds to just get people across the line, which I’ll talk about more, but we thread it through the entire “gestalt” of our organization.

John Featherston: What are some of the ground-level tactics that you’re using in your organization?

Katey McGrath: One of the things we do is we train up. If you get a call for a rental, find out if they are capable of qualifying for homeownership. We lean on our lenders. I rely on them and have a high level of expectation that they’re going to understand the down payment programs and the grant programs and the ability to stack them. We have a program called Building Equity where we crowdfund it. The partners of the company seeded it and now every agent in my company gives $5 to $50 every time they sell a house. We have a nice little fund, and we make a gift to anyone who buys a house for $250,000 or less in the city of Philadelphia. The only question we ask is, are you going to move into it?

We find that we can leverage that. If our lenders want to participate in the program and be on our website, they have to match that gift. We just want to keep the level of homeownership in Philadelphia as high as possible. And we also want people to consider other neighborhoods, other house sizes and conditions that maybe the people saving up for their dream homes are not looking at.

John Featherston: Ennis, how do you educate agents to help them find homes their buyers afford?

Ennis Antoine: When talking to my agents, I have to remind them first, you have to learn to stack resources. And what that means is, get involved in the city, the county and third-party companies like Georgia Dreams and ask them, “What programs do you have available to assist with down payment assistance?” In Atlanta, we have a program where the mayor wants to have 20,000 affordable homes built by 2030, so he has instructed his people to have this agency set aside funds to help buyers with down payment assistance; you have to live in our community for five years and it’s forgivable where you don’t have to pay back those funds. The goal is educating your agents on what funds are available and then once they’re educated, educate the buyers on what to expect and to set realistic expectations.

John Featherston: Are you seeing or anticipating any improvement in affordability issues from the ROAD to Housing Act?

Ennis Antoine: I chaired the FPC advisory committee (Federal Political Coordinators under NAR), and we worked on that bill for two years and got it passed. Now here’s the key, though. It is only an incentive. It’s going to take each one of us to inform our city councilmen and mayors on what’s available, and to pass these bills to say, “Hey, listen, how can we incentivize people to buy a home?” And then second, when it comes to housing supply, that’s going to take a while because we have an inventory shortage. It’s not going to happen overnight, but we have to be patient because it’s only a framework on what could happen if we partner with our city council and Realtor® organizations.

John Featherston: Ken, why is it critical to approach the affordability issue as far as you can see? And is it relevant to the specific markets that you’re now serving?

Ken Baris: Affordability is relative. Somebody who says “I can’t afford” is maybe a kid who grew up in a town, can’t afford to be in the town now, but they may be able to afford in another community. It’s being able to understand the benefits people can get. So for instance, Bank of America’s community reinvestment program with a grant of $17,500. We have a mortgage partnership, and we make sure anyone who will qualify for that is going to get that grant and use Bank of America because it’s good sense for the clients.

And if you are really astute about the business, you have people who are tenants—they don’t know they can afford to purchase. You can train people to purchase. You can help people improve their credit: Higher credit score, lower interest rate. You can train people to do things like say, “I will fall in like with four properties. I will not fall in love with one.” Because if you fall in like with four and we make four lower offers, we actually can turn you into a buyer and something more affordable by being willing to present offers. So we inspire a team to do the work and take the time and good things happen for clients.

We use foyersavings.com. A very interesting website; it has three things. Number one, it gives you an ability to save money at an okay interest rate or a good interest rate so that your money builds. Number two, it gives a modest down payment assistance with $600 credit of the first $10,000 you have, you get 6% additional in interest back. That’s not huge, but it’s something.

And three, it shows programs from all over—banks, lenders, community program—that provide grants. You may not know all the programs in your own market that are available. Foyer goes after these programs and makes them available to people that use the site. So it’s just being aware of these things, using your method of communication to get the information out, inspiring people to understand what they can do. If you don’t buy somewhere, you’re going to make somebody else wealthier.

John Featherston: A follow up to that, because you’re going into a lot of the nuances that help new buyers enter the marketplace. Have you made a concerted effort within your firm to make this type of training and education a competitive differentiator in your organization?

Ken Baris: Hugely. I find units to be sexy, not just high prices. And if you have salespeople that are in more affordable communities and they’re trained for these programs, they do better. Another thing that we’ll do is we’ll send out emails of successful buyers. “John thought he was going to rent. We let him know that we thought he could purchase, and the good news for John is we were right. You might be in the same position. Let’s get together.” And that’s the kind of communication we’re doing. I can’t change somebody’s income, but I could help them learn how to save more, how to improve their credit and how to get down payment assistance. $17,500 can make somebody from not a buyer to a buyer. And it’s a gift. It’s not a loan.

John Featherston: How are you and your agents getting past the current rhetoric that we hear among young people when they say they’re never going to be able to buy a home?

Katey McGrath: One of the biggest myths is that you think you need 20% down. And so it’s education, education, education, myth busting, destigmatizing these programs. It’s super important for young people in your community, but also make sure that your agents feel that way. And it’s great because like I said, the younger agents eat it up and it keeps them busy early in their career.

Ennis Antoine: I put pen to paper. So as far as paying $2,000 a month in rent, I’m saying, let’s talk about this for a second. A landlord just received $24,000 from you for one year. You say I’m staying there for three or four years. Then you have nothing to show for it. Whereas if you bought a home or a condominium, you pay this amount each month, you would have a tax write off and within four or five years, you’ll see a 4% or 5% increase in the value of the property. You can sell that property, walk away with cash, get the tax write off on your tax returns. And so if it was me, I would buy and invest and start to build wealth.

And if you build wealth, you can get a larger home and pay less money. So the key here is you’re a smart person. Let’s make a smart decision. Let’s buy.

Keith Smith: I want to pivot a little bit. We’re talking about how we can make a difference. Just last year through a land trust we put together 40 permanent affordable new construction units. I’m in Charlottesville with the second-highest cost of living in the state of Virginia, the second-highest cost of housing in Virginia. But we were able to do 40 of them. And the way we did this is what I call the four pillars: The local government, the private sector folks—developers, builders, real estate agents, the nonprofits and the people all of us serve. You got to get them into a room. You’ve got to get them all to go into the conversation. We put buyers and sellers together. We negotiate deals together. We put people together that maybe do not want to talk to one another, but they talk to people that get to the end result. And how you put those four pillars together is you show up to the meetings and you do what we all do every day very well, which is negotiate and put people together.

John Featherston: Why isn’t the real estate community playing a more pivotal role than every one of the communities, perhaps the most critical role as far as supporting homeownership?

Katey McGrath: I think everybody in this room is a connector. It’s what we love about what we do. And I think that our credibility and our expertise can help save money in these instances. The earlier we get involved in these conversations, the less mistakes the people with good intentions are going to make to make things more expensive. But also, the credibility that we have as a community member, right? So people are coming to us to buy houses, people are coming to us for education, people are coming to us to build generational wealth for their family. And then we can go to city council, we can go to the state reps, we can go to the zoning meetings and add all of that to just sort of be both sides of the issue.

Housing is bipartisan, so if you can get people together, you have that credibility, everything just becomes more productive and less expensive.

John Featherston: Getting people together over the issue of housing is a common denominator all of us can agree on. When Ennis said, local teachers, first responders, police, essential services, can’t afford to live in the community they’re serving, that is not a unique problem. That’s a problem that permeates around the nation. So the solutions have to be done locally.

Ennis Antoine: That’s correct. So I remind everyone, it doesn’t matter what company you work for, there is a percentage in every company where you deal with first-time homebuyers. It doesn’t have to be your main part of your business, but it should be a part of your business because to whom much is given, much is required. And we must always lead by example because the goal here is homeownership. What can we do? It’s all an education process. In every office, there are agents who are very passionate about their community. Support them, enhance them, show up when they need some help.

They will find a surgeon to have vibrant communities. We need a mixture of people in the community who are willing to work together, live together because we call it a village. And as real estate professionals, we are the fiber of the community. We are the voice of real estate and private property rights do matter.

Ken Baris: Something interesting we did some years ago, we listed 300 brand new two-family homes in Newark, New Jersey. And they were beautiful. The challenge was getting people in. So we had the builder prearrange financing, and we had them buy down the rate. And so it was a much lower interest rate, which lowered the payments. And then we also had the builder give a brand-new computer to every purchaser for one of the units because many of them were going to have kids and they would not have money left over for a new computer. And we thought that was very important. And then when certain buyers were tight, we then created a program where they were giving 5% toward closing costs, and if you get people to pay money toward closing costs, you also make it more affordable.

Keith Smith: “Connected” was the right word. I’ve been in this space for 15 years, and I would hear from elected officials, “Well, I don’t understand what the developer is saying.” The developer’s saying, “I don’t understand what the elected official is saying.” And then the nonprofits don’t understand anybody, and the poor folks that we’re trying to serve are left out there in the dark. Being a connector, that is the perfect word. That’s what we do. We connect and are able to put those four pillars together and put a developer and an elected official who really wants to do the right thing, together. The seller doesn’t trust the buyer; the buyer doesn’t trust the seller. We connect and we put people together and just get that conversation rolling. That’s how you do 40 new construction units in the second-highest cost-of-living area in the state of Virginia and everybody walks away smiling. I didn’t do anything really genius. I just put people in the room and said, start talking.

John Featherston: If you could do one thing to help move this affordability issue forward, what would you do?

Ennis Antoine: The one thing I would do is educate my colleagues and challenge them to get involved. It’s easy to write a check, but it’s amazing what happens when you show up. As a leader, when we show up, our people will follow. So as leaders, show up.

Ken Baris: I think just doing a better job of educating consumers because there’s a lot of buyers that don’t know their buyers. Not everyone will be able to afford. They’ve never always been able to, but there’s many more out there.

Katey McGrath: I’m going to go a little more philosophical. Just remember how important homeownership is to every metric in the community. It reduces crime. It increases education rates. It can lower the temperature in a zip code. It extends life expectancy, but most importantly, it builds generational wealth and creates health outcomes in that community that lift everybody up. And if you internalize that, you’re going to be happier when you go to work. You’re going to have more patience to deal with the hard clients that you’re not going to make a lot of money on and just feel great at the end of the day.

Keith Smith: Invest the one asset you can’t make more of, which is your time. Show up and over time, you’ll make a difference. And of those affordable housing units, every single key I handed to somebody, they were in tears. They never thought they were going to get into the homeownership game. It’s not about the check. It’s about the tears, and it makes a difference.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5622. Don Jr’s Investor Business Partner Abruptly Resigns from Fannie Mae Board

Conservative businessman Omeed Malik, a close Trump ally and business partner of Donald Trump Jr., has stepped down from the board of Fannie Mae.

The government-sponsored mortgage giant said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday that Malik resigned from the board of directors, effective October 30. Malik is president of the venture capital firm 1789 Capital as well as founder of investment bank Farvahar Partners. Trump Jr. joined 1789 as a partner in November of 2024.

Malik provided "brings extensive experience in financial services and capital markets as well as a blend of legal, entrepreneurial, and strategic leadership expertise," Fannie said in its last annual report in February. He was paid $114,222 last year, that filing shows.

As a member of the eight-member board, Malik has been a part of Fannie Mae as it has enlarged its balance sheet at the behest of President Donald Trump, who pushed the GSE to buy mortgage-backed securities in a bid to lower mortgage rates.

Trump has also floated the idea of ending the conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, potentially setting the stage for a $30 billion IPO. But the Trump administration has said little of those plans in recent months as Americans grapple with inflation and rising housing costs.

Malik joined the board in April 2025. At the time, Federal Housing Administrator Bill Pulte, who chairs the board, posted to X "Omeed brings great capital markets, legal and investment experience as we Make Fannie and Freddie Great Again!"

Fannie Mae reported $4.2 billion in net income in the third quarter. This year it has provided about $344 billion in liquidity to 295,000 homebuyers. The company's overall net worth has swelled from $47.4 billion in 2021 to $119.6 billion in the third quarter.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5621. Apple’s stock drops as new CEO John Ternus delivers his first earnings call

Apple Inc. just delivered its first earnings call since new Chief Executive John Ternus took over the company from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, and the results beat expectations on the top and bottom lines. But the company missed expectations on iPhone sales and offered disappointing guidance going forward, and the stock fell in late trading.

The company reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.10 per share, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s target of $1.99 per share. Revenue for the period rose 12%, to $114.48 billion, easing past the $113.39 billion analyst forecast. All told, its net income came to $30.71 billion at the end of the quarter, up from just $27.46 billion one year earlier.

When Ternus (pictured) stepped up to relieve Cook in the CEO’s chair a couple of months ago, he realized he was stepping into a job with sky-high expectations, following in the footsteps of two of the most successful company leaders in American history. Steve Jobs was credited with revolutionizing consumer devices, while Cook took the company to spectacular new heights thanks to his operational expertise, establishing it as one of the world’s most iconic brands.

The weight of expectations is reflected by Apple’s enormous valuation. According to Oppenheimer analyst Martin Yang, the iPhone maker is trading at about 36 times next year’s expected earnings. That represents a premium compared with the rest of the technology market, even though its earnings are only expected to grow 1% this year, slower than many of its peers.

Nonetheless, investors have piled into Apple because it’s something of an outlier in the artificial intelligence boom. While its rivals are all spending hundreds of billions of dollars on building data centers, Apple has remained extremely capital-efficient, pouring cash into share buybacks and dividends for shareholders. That has given the company a strong margin for safety, but its position could still be threatened if Ternus can’t find a way to speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

The company has already been criticized for its lackluster performance in AI. Its long-awaited Siri AI chatbot finally arrived during the past quarter, but it came across as stale the moment it arrived. By the time it had launched, it had already been surpassed by autonomous AI agents such as Dots and Muse that can perform multistep tasks on behalf of users, while Siri is still fumbling around with answering questions.

Analysts wanted to know if Apple is planning to offer more AI features through subscriptions or services, but Ternus declined to reveal what the company’s future plans are. But he insisted that Apple has “lots of opportunities” for monetization in future. “One example is the hardware side, right?” he said. “It offers a compelling reason for upgrading or switching.”

Jacob Bourne of Emarketer told SiliconANGLE that Apple’s stock premium is likely linked to the growing concerns some investors have over the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom, which is being driven by all of Apple’s big tech peers. “Its tepid approach to AI infrastructure spending has helped to preserve its cash flow, and through strategic partnerships Apple may be able to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers,” Bourne said. “But Apple faces its own challenges as AI-enabled devices such as smart glasses could eventually challenge the iPhone’s central role in iOS. Apple’s long-term advantage will hinge on combining its hardware strengths with compelling AI capabilities in a way that preserves its reputation.”

In the meantime, the pressure is on for Apple to give consumers more reasons to buy its expensive devices, especially as the costs of those products have been getting higher. Today’s report was the first full quarter of higher-priced Apple products following a price hike in June that stemmed from the rising cost of memory supplies and other components.

The price of most iPhone handsets was hiked by around $100, but consumers didn’t appear to punish Apple. On the contrary, iPhone revenue was a bright spot, reaching $57.58 billion in the quarter, up 17% from a year earlier and above the $56.54 billion consensus estimate. That’s despite the quarter including only eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales and none of the new flagship device, the iPhone Duo.

Apple needed a good quarter from the iPhone because its main growth engine, the services business, is slowing. Revenue there came to $31.57 billion, just below the Street’s forecast of $31.58 billion, growing less than 10% during the quarter, its slowest rate of growth since September 2022. The business includes revenue from a wide range of products and services, such as iCloud storage, AppleCare warranties, App Store fees and licensing revenue from Google LLC for putting its search engine as the default option in the Safari browser.

“We saw strong performance in many service categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, and a September quarter record in music,” Tetanus told analysts.

Apple saw a better performance in its Mac computer division, with sales of $10.79 billion comfortably topping the Street’s forecast of $9.61 billion. The unit’s revenue grew almost 24% on an annual basis, following the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac Mini laptops in August.

The iPad division was a disaster, however, as sales declined more than 10% from the previous year to $6.3 billion, trailing the Street’s forecast of $6.7 billion. Last month saw the launch of a new iPad Mini model, following the debut of the updated iPad Air back in March, but despite those releases, there has been no flagship model launching this year, and that appears to have hurt the business’ performance. When asked about the miss, Ternus blamed supply constraints and a difficult comparison with last year as the main reasons for its disappointing performance.

The disappointing performance of Apple’s services and iPad units was compounded by what was seen as weak guidance for the current quarter, which includes the peak Christmas sales period. Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh didn’t offer concrete numbers, but said the company expects its revenue to grow by between 7% and 10% in the quarter. Wall Street analysts are looking for higher growth of 11.4%, however. Parekh also revealed that Apple is forecasting its gross margin to fall between 45% and 46%, declining from the fourth quarter.

Apple’s stock fell almost 3% on today’s report, but it’s still up more than 24% in the year to date compared with a gain of just over 10% for the broader S&P 500 index.
