#5604. 8 foods that may help you sleep, from tart cherries to chamomile tea

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tart cherries, night milk, kiwi, and chamomile tea appear among 8 foods the Sleep Foundation links to better rest.

Anyone who has gulped a second cup of coffee to survive a long afternoon, or dozed on the couch after Thanksgiving dinner, has felt food tilt a person toward alertness or drowsiness. The same plate that props up a workday can shape the hours after dark. Diet and sleep are both intricate systems, and each one reaches into the other. No single snack guarantees a quiet night, and nothing on a grocery shelf works as a magic switch. Certain foods and drinks may make a full night of rest easier to reach. Some contain nutrients and compounds that influence sleep-related hormones and brain activity, from melatonin production to blood sugar levels that hold steady overnight.

The body's sleep chemistry depends on what arrives on the plate. Melatonin, a hormone the pineal gland produces, signals when sleep should begin and keeps the circadian rhythm on schedule, and its output tends to fall with age. Tryptophan, an essential amino acid, must come from food because the body cannot make it. The body converts it into melatonin and into serotonin, a neurotransmitter tied to sleep, mood, and pain. Carbohydrates help the brain process tryptophan. The wrong late-night choices can undercut these processes. Citrus, tomatoes, and other acidic foods can raise stomach acid and bring on reflux. One study found that caffeine a person drank six hours before bed still affected sleep quality, and the stimulant has an average half-life of five hours in most healthy adults. Whole foods may hold advantages over pills. They deliver vitamins, minerals, and micronutrients that work in concert, along with fiber, which tracks with deeper sleep, and antioxidants that help ward off disease. Anyone weighing a supplement to fill a nutritional gap should consult a health care provider before starting it.

Sleep Foundation built its guide to sleep-friendly foods and drinks on 24 references, most of them published studies, and reports no original testing of its own. Eric Suni wrote the piece, which bears an Aug. 5, 2025, update date. Lulu Guo, MD, a board-certified sleep medicine physician, reviewed it for medical accuracy. Guo urges readers to focus on healthy eating patterns across the whole day instead of pinning their hopes on one food or drink. The guide sorts its picks by the nutrient they supply, with sections for melatonin, tryptophan, and magnesium and a fourth set of foods that work through other compounds. It lists foods to skip before bed and answers common questions about supplements and caffeine timing. Advertising supports the site, which says it does not endorse third-party products. The eight foods that follow form a selection from that longer guide, in the order the source presents them, and they appear without any ranking.

Tart cherries hold above-average concentrations of melatonin, the hormone that cues sleep, and the Sleep Foundation names that trait as one possible reason the fruit may help people doze off. Some shoppers know them as sour cherries, a label that captures how their flavor departs from the sweet varieties. The group spans several cultivars, among them Richmond, Montmorency, and English morello.

Grocers stock the fruit whole or pressed into tart cherry juice. Bakers reach for the tart type in pies and other baked goods, and fresh tart cherries can be tough to find, according to Cleveland Clinic. Scarce fresh fruit explains why most recommendations steer people toward the juice over the whole cherry. A bottle gives the easiest entry point for anyone hoping to test the fruit at bedtime.

Several studies have found that people who drink tart cherry juice sleep better. Melatonin may not account for the whole benefit. The Sleep Foundation adds that the cherries may exert an antioxidant action that favors sleep, a second possible route to a better night.

A Cleveland Clinic expert noted that tart cherries also contain tryptophan. The expert called it plausible that the amino acid and the fruit's melatonin could help people relax and sleep better. The body converts tryptophan into melatonin, which means each serving may deliver the hormone itself along with a building block for more.

Cleveland Clinic reports that early research on the juice has been small and short on rigor. The small studies suggest the drink may lengthen sleep and improve its quality, and scientists need more work to confirm the signal. The Cleveland Clinic expert cautioned that strong scientific evidence for a sleep benefit is still lacking. Two candidate mechanisms and a string of encouraging findings make tart cherries a credible bedtime option, one still built on early evidence.

Milk drawn at night holds nearly 10 times more melatonin than milk collected during the day. The evening yield goes by the name night milk, and the Sleep Foundation identifies milking time as a major influence on how much of the sleep hormone the drink contains. Flip the comparison and a daytime glass carries about one-tenth of the melatonin in an equal pour of night milk.

The gap turns milk into a drink whose sleep chemistry shifts with the clock. Two glasses can look identical yet differ several times over in the hormone that cues the body to wind down. Among the foods the Sleep Foundation credits with melatonin, milk stands out because the hour of collection helps set the dose.

Night milk produced calming, sedative, and sleep-promoting effects in mice, and researchers likened its impact to diazepam. The result comes from animal research and cannot predict how people will respond. Even so, the mouse findings suggest the extra hormone in evening milk can do measurable work in a living body.

Warm milk at bedtime has a long history as a home remedy, and the Sleep Foundation argues that real science supports the drink as a sleep aid. A heated mug may also help through comfort. If a warm cup relaxes someone as part of a nightly routine, it could ease the way to sleep even when the benefit amounts to a placebo.

Milk offers two separate paths to rest. One runs through the melatonin it carries, a supply concentrated in milk drawn after dark. The other runs through the soothing habit of a warm drink before bed, which can work whatever the hormone count. A sleeper chasing the chemical benefit would gain the most from night milk, while the ritual benefit asks for nothing more than a warm mug and a bedtime routine.

Fatty fish supplies vitamin D and omega-3 fatty acids, two nutrients researchers believe can help people sleep. Each one has a hand in how the body releases serotonin and keeps its levels in balance.

Fish also turns up on the Sleep Foundation's list of tryptophan sources, next to turkey, chicken, eggs, cheese, edamame, tofu, peanuts, quinoa, and pumpkin seeds. The amino acid serves as raw material for serotonin, so a single serving touches two stages of the same chain. Tryptophan builds the neurotransmitter, and vitamin D and omega-3s help govern its release.

Pairing fish with carbohydrates may give its tryptophan a clearer path. The guide says a moderate portion of tryptophan-bearing protein eaten alongside carbs may help the amino acid reach the brain. It traces the drowsiness people blame on turkey to that same pairing. A fish fillet over rice fits the pattern the source sets out for poultry.

The guide presents the fish benefit as a belief researchers hold and attaches no serving size or expected effect to it. Fatty fish earns its place through nutrients that act on serotonin from both ends, though the guide leaves the size of any sleep payoff unmeasured.

Cheese delivers a high dose of tryptophan, and the Sleep Foundation credits that amino acid with most of the sleep benefit linked to dairy. Some research has found a strong connection between dairy foods such as cheese and the quality of a person's rest, the guide reports.

Cheese appears on the guide's quick-reference list of tryptophan sources, alongside turkey, chicken, fish, eggs, edamame, tofu, peanuts, quinoa, and pumpkin seeds. It stands as the lone milk-based entry among those 10 foods. The listing gives people who skip meat and fish one more option, beside eggs and plant foods such as tofu, for an evening meal or snack.

Tryptophan gives cheese a sleep pathway separate from milk's, whose appeal in the guide hinges on the melatonin it holds. The guide's entry on cheese names no melatonin content and leans mainly on the amino acid, which hands the body raw material for building its own sleep chemistry. The entry also points to serotonin, calcium, and selenium, a mineral whose antioxidant properties may improve sleep. Cheese thus arrives with one finished sleep compound, serotonin, alongside the building block, plus a mineral that works on a separate front.

Calcium turns up in milk and yogurt as well as cheese, and the body draws on the mineral to turn tryptophan into melatonin. AARP reports that nutritionist Bonnie Taub-Dix called cheese a protein-rich snack and said its calcium, magnesium, and tryptophan are all needed for good sleep. Her list adds magnesium to the nutrients a wedge of cheese brings to the plate.

Carbohydrates may ease the trip cheese's tryptophan makes into the brain, according to the guide, which says a moderate serving of tryptophan-bearing protein eaten with carbs may smooth that route. Its turkey section explains that carbohydrates help the amino acid cross the blood-brain barrier and lift serotonin levels. One bedtime snack idea tops whole-grain crackers with cheese. Such a pairing places protein and carbohydrate in the same bite, the mix the guide describes. Cheese eaten alone may do less for sleep than cheese eaten with a starch.

One cup of firm tofu holds 593 milligrams of tryptophan, which equals 212% of the recommended daily intake. A single cup of the firm block more than doubles a full day's target for the amino acid.

Soy foods appear twice on the Sleep Foundation's quick list of tryptophan sources, as edamame and as tofu. The list also names turkey, chicken, fish, eggs, cheese, peanuts, quinoa, and pumpkin seeds. Plants supply half of its 10 entries. Diners who skip meat or dairy can reach the amino acid through soy, which the guide describes as a group of foods with solid amounts of it.

Tofu's tryptophan may go further with a starchy partner. Elsewhere in the guide, the Sleep Foundation notes that a moderate amount of tryptophan-bearing protein eaten alongside carbohydrates may help the amino acid reach the brain. Its turkey entry makes the same point from another angle, crediting carbohydrates with helping tryptophan cross the blood-brain barrier and lift serotonin levels. Tofu served with rice, another food the guide covers, fits that pattern.

Soybeans carry isoflavones, a class of phytoestrogen. In the guide's account, these plant compounds may mimic human estrogen, a hormone that helps govern how long and how well people sleep. The source treats this hormonal link as a possibility and stops short of calling it proven. Its wording puts the isoflavone claim on softer footing than the tofu figure, which arrives as a measured quantity.

Soy may act on rest through two separate routes, supplying tryptophan in quantity while its isoflavones work on a hormonal pathway of their own. Among the eight foods in this selection, it stands alone in reaching sleep through an estrogen-like compound.

One cup of uncooked oats packs 66% of the daily value for magnesium and 130% of the recommended daily intake for tryptophan. The tryptophan share overshoots a full day's target by 30 percentage points, which means a single bowl meets the day's entire need for the amino acid and leaves a surplus. The magnesium share falls a fraction short of two-thirds of a day's requirement in the same serving. Oats hold close to double the magnesium and five times the tryptophan of a cup of boiled spinach, which the guide credits with 37% of the daily value for magnesium and 26% of the recommended intake for tryptophan.

Complex carbohydrates give oats a second sleep mechanism. The Sleep Foundation reports that these carbohydrates lift serotonin and reduce cortisol, a stress hormone capable of interfering with sleep. Turkey, by the guide's account, needs carbohydrates beside it on the plate to produce its familiar drowsiness. Oats bring the amino acid and the carbohydrates to the table in one food, with no side dish necessary. The guide tempers the carbohydrate case with a caveat, noting that research on carbohydrates and sleep has produced mixed results.

Old-fashioned, quick-cooking, and instant oats all belong to the rolled oat family, and thinner rolling shortens the time on the stove. Old-fashioned oats take the longest of the three and reward the wait with a heartier, chewier texture. Steel cut oats, also known as Irish oats, skip steaming and rolling and require more simmering than any other variety. Water and milk both work as the base liquid, while stock or broth turns the pot savory.

Overnight oats call for little or no heat. Old-fashioned or quick-cooking oats soak through the night in low-fat milk, then take a topping of fruit.

Oats supply plenty of fiber and several B vitamins, a profile they hold in common with barley, farro, and brown rice. The Sleep Foundation counts fiber among the whole-food advantages tied to deeper, more restorative sleep. Measured against the guide's own nutrient framework, oats reach three of its four sleep pathways: tryptophan, magnesium, and complex carbohydrates.

Two kiwis eaten an hour before bedtime helped people drift off sooner, stay asleep longer, and give their rest higher marks, according to the Sleep Foundation. The gains reach three separate stretches of the night. Falling asleep, staying asleep, and the perceived quality of slumber all improved in the same finding. One small snack touched the start, the length, and the feel of a night in bed.

Kiwifruit packs numerous vitamins and minerals. The Sleep Foundation singles out four standouts: vitamins C and E, potassium, and folate. A fruit eaten before lights-out brings that payload along with whatever influence it has on sleep.

Nobody has pinned down why kiwi helps. Researchers suspect antioxidant properties that suppress inflammatory markers. The fruit may correct folate deficiencies or act through serotonin, and some mix of these could account for the effect.

Folate links two threads of the evidence. The nutrient appears among kiwi's featured contents, and one candidate explanation credits the fruit with making up for a shortage of that same nutrient. People low in folate could gain the most if that theory holds.

Serotonin connects kiwi to a pathway the guide traces through several other foods. Cheese, tofu, and oats supply tryptophan, the raw material the body uses to build that neurotransmitter. Kiwi carries a high concentration of serotonin itself, and scientists count the trait among the possible reasons for its benefit. If the idea proves out, the fruit would arrive with the finished compound in hand, while those foods offer the building block.

Among the eight foods in this selection, kiwi alone comes with both a set portion and a set time to eat it. Tofu and oats list serving sizes, yet neither includes advice on when to eat. With the cause unsettled, the timing becomes the most usable part of the result. Anyone can copy a pair of fruit an hour before bed without waiting for the science to catch up.

Chamomile tea owes its drowsy reputation to apigenin, a flavonoid the Sleep Foundation identifies as the compound thought to bring on the effect. The plant chemical has anxiolytic and sedative properties, which allow it to act on the central nervous system. A cup may ease anxiety and help the body unwind.

Apigenin sets the drink apart from most other foods in this selection. Tart cherries, milk, tofu, and oats earn attention for melatonin, tryptophan, or magnesium, nutrients tied to the hormones and brain chemistry that govern sleep. Chamomile follows a separate path. Its flavonoid targets the restless, keyed-up state that can hold off slumber.

The Sleep Foundation frames apigenin's role as a working theory, and research in people lends that theory some weight. AARP reports that a 2017 study tested chamomile extract on adults age 60 and older. The group taking the extract posted significant gains in sleep quality over a placebo group. Hunnes, an expert in the same AARP feature, also credits apigenin with encouraging sleepiness, which puts the outlet's account in line with the Sleep Foundation's.

The study measured an extract, not a brewed cup, so the dose a mug of tea delivers remains an open question. Its participants also came from a single age group. Chamomile's clearest promise lies in calming an anxious mind before bed, and the firmest human evidence for it so far comes from older adults.

#5603. Why Offerpad is getting more selective on home buys

Offerpad said faster rising mortgage rates and affordability pressures slowed home sales in Q3 2026. The iBuyer tightened acquisition criteria, leaned more on brokerage and its marketplace and guided to positive adjusted EBITDA run rate by Q2 2027.  AI Summary

Heading into the second half of 2026, Offerpad was laser-focused on “turning its buying engine back on,” however, housing market headwinds caused by rapidly rising mortgage rates and continued affordability challenges, have led the iBuyer to increase the intentionality behind its strategy.

In a call with investors and analysts to discuss the company’s third quarter 2026 earnings, Offerpad executives said that with homes taking longer to sell, the firm adjusted its acquisition criteria to require higher expected returns on a property. In addition, they said the company has become more selective about new purchases and that it adjusted its underwriting to build wider expected margins into each purchase.

Instead of providing home sellers with a direct cash offer, executives said Offerpad was looking to serve more sellers through its Cash Offer Marketplace and Brokerage Services offerings.

During the quarter, Offerpad recorded 324 total transactions, up from 295 transactions a quarter prior, but down 32% annually. Executives attributed the lower-than-anticipated number of transactions for the quarter to the overall slower housing market.

“We’ve operated with mortgage rates above 7% before,” Brian Bair, the CEO of Offerpad, said during the earnings call Monday evening. “What was different this time was the speed of the move late in our quarter and the attention it received. Housing affordability has become a national story. With headlines describing it as a buyer’s market. Buyers weighed higher monthly payments against the possibility of a better deal. While sellers faced uncertainty about how long their homes would take to sell and what price they could achieve. We believe that combination contributed to a more cautious market as the quarter came to a close.”

In total, Offerpad’s Brokerage Services and Cash Offer Marketplace represented approximately 35% of Q3 closed transactions, with the company noting that brokerage listing signings more than doubled from Q2 2026.

In total, Offerpad acquired 605 homes during the quarter, up 198% annually. According to executives, these purchases were concentrated in markets where homes were still selling at a pace that met the company’s requirements. On the sales side, Offerpad sold 210 homes during the quarter, down 43% annually, but up slightly from Q2 2026.

“Last quarter, we said we were increasing acquisitions and we did by acquiring 605 homes in Q3. We also had additional homes under contract that could have increased that total. As market conditions shifted, we reevaluated them against our wider margin requirements and chose not to proceed with homes that no longer met our criteria,” Bair, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said. “Where possible, we offered those sellers an alternative through cash offer or broker services. Buying well is only half the process.”

At the end of the quarter aged inventory represented just 2.6% of all homes on the balance sheet, well below Offerpad’s 10% aged inventory threshold. The company said that this inventory is expected to provide a pipeline of dispositions through the rest of 2026 and into early 2027. So far in Q4, leaders said 200 homes have sold or are under contract for sale.

Bair noted on the call that Offerpad’s current portfolio of homes is “healthy” and that most were bought within the last few months.

Looking ahead, Offerpad executives said that returning to profitability is the company’s primary focus. During the third quarter of 2026, Offerpad recorded $78.1 million in revenue, down 41% annually, while the company’s net loss of $11.5 million for the quarter was a 1% improvement compared to a year prior. As the iBuyer looks to get back into the black, executives said they are focused on reducing operating expenses and growing Cash Offer Marketplace and brokerage services.

While the company has cut operating expenses by more than $140 million since 2022, during Q3, executives said they identified an additional $8 million to $10 million in annualized operating expense reductions, which they expect to be implemented in 2027.

“Profitability remains our No. 1 priority. And nothing about that has changed. What has changed is the timeline. The shift in the market has pushed our path out, and we now expect to exit the second quarter of 2027 at a positive adjusted EBITDA run rate,” Bair said. “Together, these actions give us the opportunity to reach positive adjusted EBITDA with fewer transactions than before.”

Offerpad executives have noted that they believe positive adjusted EBITDA will come with roughly 1,000 transactions per quarter. In Q4 2026, the company said it anticipated 400-475 transactions, but executives are optimistic the firm will reach that 1,000 transaction threshold. On the call, executives noted that the firm is using lenders to fund a larger share of each home’s cost, meaning that less of Offerpad’s capital is tied up in the homes the firm buys.

“That makes our capital go further and it helps it return to the business faster as homes sell. At quarter end, we had approximately $251 million of undrawn capacity under our inventory financing facilities, the majority of which is uncommitted,” Andrew Piper, who was appointed interim chief financial officer, replacing Peter Knag, said. “We believe our cash, the capital we expect to return as homes sell, and our inventory financing are sufficient as we execute our 2027 plan. We also remain open to opportunities to strengthen our balance sheet, including strategic capital partnerships, and we will be disciplined about the structure and cost of any capital we add.”

#5602. Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI

How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?

This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.

Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.

Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.

“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”

A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.

Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.

“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”

Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.

Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.

The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.

“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”

A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.

Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.

“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”

In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.

This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.

“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”

Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.

“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”

#5601. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5599. Mortgage rates have a quiet week as markets digest Fed comments, Trump’s directive

Mortgage rates were mostly flat week over week, with the 30-year fixed averaging 7.38%. Jumbo and FHA rates fell modestly, while markets are still pricing a likely 25-bps Fed hike in December.  AI Summary

Mortgage rate movement was largely flat in the past week, with the downward momentum of previous weeks cooling off even as more potential homebuyers have been incentivized to seek financing.

At HousingWire’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year loans averaged 7.38% — the same as one week ago. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.62%, down 7 bps in a week, while 30-year rates for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans stood at 7.16%, down 8 bps.

The small declines in rates come a week after the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate at a range of 3.75% of 4% in a widely expected decision. But after policymakers hiked rates in September, further increases are anticipated, with the CME Group’s FedWatch tool showing that 77% of interest rate traders predict a 25-basis-point increase in December.

HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote this week that tighter monetary policy “has created financial pain for some AI companies.” With the Fed focusing on the inflationary aspects of AI and associated debt-financing issues, the 10-year Treasury yield has been dropping, which has placed downward pressure on mortgage rates.

Hector Amendola, president of Las Vegas-based mortgage lender SimplyPMG, told HousingWire in an interview that he believes a December hike is already baked into current rates and that drastic movement, up or down, is unlikely to happen for the rest of this year.

“It’s kind of been par for the course now for a while, that rates are continuing to rise based on the expectation that the Fed will go up a little bit more until there’s a way to figure out how to tame inflation a little bit,” Amendola said.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced last week that the central bank would be shifting to fewer policy votes in each of the next two years. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) currently meets eight times a year, with a vote scheduled after each, but the number of votes will be reduced to seven in 2027 and potentially to six in 2028.

“I think it puts a little bit more weight on each of the meetings,” he said. “I also think it’s interesting, because as Warsh kicks over, you’re kind of wondering if it’ll be like, ‘Let’s break everything and see what happens and figure it out later,’ or are we going to continue to really look at the data and do what the data tells us?

“I think what I’ve seen so far is, it’s still a wait-and-see approach. Let’s see what the data says, and that’s kind of why I think this particular decision that came out [last week] was expected, because the data is saying, ‘Slow down.’”

Last month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that targets lower costs in multiple areas of housing finance. These include proactive mortgage insurance cancellations for conventional loan servicers, an expanded title waiver program through the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), reduced rates on some government-backed loans and the creation of a manufactured housing task force.

Mat Ishbia, president and CEO of United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), said this week in his monthly “3 Points” video that “housing affordability continues to be front and center in Washington D.C. There’s a real focus right now on finding ways to lower the cost of homeownership, reduce friction in the mortgage process and make financing more accessible.”

He pointed specifically to the proposal to make the title insurance waiver pilot a permanent program, saying that prior waivers on some low-risk refinances have been “saving consumers thousands of dollars.”

“Some of these ideas will help; some of them won’t help,” Ishbia said of the executive order. “We’ll see how it all shakes out. But I think these are good things they’re looking at doing.”

Amendola said his company has “always been big proponents” of waiving title insurance on refi transactions with loan-to-value ratios below 80%. “Like, what are we really doing? It’s the same consumer. You know, all that stuff is still coming up,” he remarked.

He also said that allowing servicers of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans to help borrowers cancel their mortgage insurance premiums when they reach the statutory threshold “is a bigger deal than people think.” U.S. Mortgage Insurers have expressed their support for the move, while some analysts label it as “fairly benign” for the financial performance of mortgage insurers.

“That’s extra revenue that they’re making right now that they, honestly, probably shouldn’t be making — and suddenly they’re going to have an impact on their end,” Amendola said. “But it’s going to be really good for the homeowner to free up some of that cash that can then turn into something else for them.”

#5598. Colorado to Vermont: the 8 states that still tax Social Security benefits

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Eight states tax Social Security benefits in 2026, each with its own rules on who pays, plus how federal taxation works and how West Virginia left the list

Social Security benefits face two separate tax systems, and they rarely line up. At the federal level, up to 85 percent of a retiree's benefits can count as taxable income, depending on a figure called combined income. The income thresholds that trigger the tax date to 1983 and 1993. They have never been indexed to inflation. The same dollar lines that applied decades ago still apply today.

Most states take the opposite approach and leave benefits untaxed. The states that tax Social Security benefits in 2026 are Colorado, Connecticut, Minnesota, Montana, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Utah and Vermont. Living in one of them does not mean a retiree automatically owes state tax on benefits. Most of these states shield lower- and middle-income households through exemptions, subtractions or credits. In several of them, those breaks shrink or disappear as income rises.

The details vary widely from state to state. Connecticut fully exempts benefits for single filers with adjusted gross income under $75,000 and joint filers under $100,000. New Mexico sets its exemption lines at $100,000 for single filers and $150,000 for joint filers. Colorado lets residents 65 and older subtract all of their federally taxable benefits. Rhode Island ties its exemption to reaching full retirement age and staying under an income limit. Utah offers a nonrefundable credit rather than an exemption.

The list has shrunk in recent years. Kansas, Missouri and Nebraska each stopped taxing Social Security benefits in 2024. West Virginia ran a three-year phaseout through 2026 and is generally listed as no longer taxing benefits this year. For retirees comparing states, how benefits are treated is only one part of the picture. Taxes on pensions, retirement account withdrawals, property and purchases also shape what a household owes.

This guide covers 10 subjects. The first explains how federal tax on benefits works. The federally taxable portion of benefits is the starting point for some state calculations. The next eight cover each state that still taxes benefits, without ranking them by tax burden. The last covers West Virginia's exit from the list. Thresholds and credit amounts can change from year to year. Each state's tax agency is the place to confirm the current figures for the tax year a retiree is filing.

Up to 85 percent of Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax, depending on a figure the IRS calls combined income. No one pays federal tax on all of their benefits. Retirees with little income beyond Social Security often owe no federal tax on their benefits at all.

Combined income has three parts. It starts with adjusted gross income. It then adds any nontaxable interest, such as interest from municipal bonds. Finally, it adds half of the year's Social Security benefits. The total is compared with fixed dollar thresholds that depend on filing status.

For single filers, benefits begin to become partly taxable once combined income passes $25,000. Between that level and $34,000, up to 50 percent of benefits can be taxed. Above $34,000, the taxable share can rise to as much as 85 percent.

Joint filers face the same two-step structure at higher levels. Their benefits become partly taxable above $32,000 in combined income. Up to 85 percent becomes taxable above $44,000.

Those percentages describe how much of the benefit counts as taxable income. They are not tax rates. The taxable portion is added to a filer's other income and taxed at ordinary federal income tax rates.

The two tiers came from separate laws a decade apart. Congress created the 50 percent tier in 1983 and added the 85 percent tier in 1993.

The money raised by each tier goes to a different place. Tax collected under the original tier is credited to the Social Security trust funds. Revenue from the higher tier goes to Medicare's Hospital Insurance trust fund.

The dollar thresholds have stayed at the levels Congress set. Annual cost-of-living adjustments, meanwhile, push benefit payments higher. That means more beneficiaries cross the thresholds over time.

The paperwork starts with Form SSA-1099, which the Social Security Administration sends each January. It shows the total benefits paid during the previous year. IRS Publication 915 includes a worksheet for working out the taxable portion.

Beneficiaries who expect to owe tax can have it withheld from their monthly payments. They do this by filing Form W-4V and choosing a withholding rate of seven, 10, 12 or 22 percent. Quarterly estimated tax payments are the other option.

The federal figures also carry over to state returns. Many state income tax returns begin with federal adjusted gross income, which already includes any taxable share of benefits. A state that taxes Social Security then applies its own exemptions, subtractions or credits to that amount.

Colorado residents 65 and older can subtract all of their federally taxable Social Security income on their state return. For filers in that age group, the subtraction removes benefits from Colorado taxable income entirely.

Colorado remains among the states that tax benefits because its break depends on age rather than income. Younger beneficiaries do not get the full subtraction.

The mechanism is a subtraction, not a blanket exemption. Colorado calculates its income tax starting from federal taxable income. Any Social Security that is taxable on a federal return therefore flows into the Colorado calculation by default. The subtraction is the line that takes it back out. A retiree has to claim it on the state return to receive the benefit.

The subtraction applies only to the federally taxable portion of benefits. That means the federal formula still determines the amount in play. A retiree whose benefits are not taxable at the federal level has nothing to subtract in Colorado.

For filers 65 and older, the Social Security subtraction has no dollar ceiling. A retiree in that age group can remove the entire federally taxable amount, whether it is small or large.

Residents aged 55 to 64 receive a more limited version. Their subtraction is capped at $20,000. That cap covers pension and annuity income, and Social Security counts toward it. A 60-year-old who collects both a pension and Social Security draws on the same $20,000 limit for both sources.

Federally taxable retirement income above that limit stays in Colorado taxable income for this age group. The cap is a fixed dollar amount. It does not grow with the size of a person's benefit.

Residents under 55 generally fall outside the age-based subtraction. Social Security Disability Insurance pays benefits to some people well before retirement age. Federally taxable benefits of that kind remain part of Colorado income for those filers.

Colorado taxes income at a single flat rate rather than through graduated brackets. Any Social Security left after the subtraction is taxed at the same rate as wages or other income. The Colorado Department of Revenue publishes the current rules and subtraction forms for each tax year.

Connecticut fully exempts Social Security benefits for single filers with adjusted gross income under $75,000 and joint filers under $100,000. Retirees above those lines still get a partial break. For them, the state can tax no more than 25 percent of their benefits.

The income test uses adjusted gross income. That is a different measure from the combined income figure the IRS uses to decide how much of a person's benefits are federally taxable. Federal adjusted gross income includes the share of benefits that is federally taxable. A retiree with large benefits can therefore move closer to the Connecticut limit through the benefits themselves.

The thresholds depend on filing status. A single filer compares adjusted gross income with the $75,000 line. A married couple filing jointly compares its joint adjusted gross income with the $100,000 line. The joint threshold is $25,000 higher than the single threshold, not twice as high.

Connecticut's 25 percent cap is far below the federal ceiling. Federal rules allow up to 85 percent of benefits to be taxed for higher-income recipients. Connecticut's limit sits 60 percentage points lower. The 25 percent figure is a maximum share of benefits, not a tax rate.

A dollar example shows the gap. Take a retiree above the state limit who collects $30,000 in Social Security benefits in a year. Up to $25,500 of that amount could be taxable on the federal return. Connecticut could tax no more than $7,500 of the same benefits. That leaves $18,000 of benefits within federal reach but outside Connecticut's.

Retirees below the limits owe no Connecticut tax on their benefits. Households with pensions, investment income or wages on top of benefits are the ones most likely to cross the thresholds. Connecticut's Department of Revenue Services administers the exemption and publishes the forms and instructions for each tax year. That agency is the place to confirm the current rules before filing.

Minnesota taxes Social Security benefits, but it lets many retirees subtract some or all of those benefits from their state taxable income. The size of that subtraction depends on income and filing status, and it shrinks as income rises.

A subtraction works differently from a tax credit. It lowers the amount of income Minnesota taxes rather than cutting the tax bill directly. The dollar value of the break therefore depends on the state tax rate that would otherwise apply to the subtracted income.

Minnesota uses a graduated income tax with four brackets. The same subtraction can be worth a different amount to two retirees, depending on which bracket the subtracted income would have fallen into.

The subtraction only reaches benefits that are already taxable at the federal level. A retiree whose benefits are not federally taxable has nothing to subtract on the state return. For that person, the Minnesota subtraction never comes into play.

Income is the main variable. Retirees with lower incomes can generally subtract more of their benefits. As income climbs, the allowable subtraction gets smaller. Past a certain income level, a retiree may receive only a partial subtraction or none at all.

The income that counts is not limited to Social Security. Pension payments, retirement account withdrawals and other taxable income all feed into the test. A larger withdrawal in one year can shrink the subtraction for that year.

Filing status also changes the calculation. Single filers, married couples filing jointly and married people filing separately face different limits. Two households with identical benefits can end up with different Minnesota tax results because of how they file.

The Minnesota Department of Revenue publishes the current income limits and the instructions used to figure the subtraction. Its figures for the 2026 tax year are the ones that apply to a 2026 return. Limits published for earlier tax years do not carry over automatically.

Montana taxes Social Security benefits in 2026, and retirees there can owe state income tax on part of what they receive. The state has also changed the method it uses to calculate the taxable amount.

That change affects anyone who files a Montana return each year. Rules from earlier tax years may not match the current ones. A filer who repeats a prior year's approach could misjudge what the 2026 state return requires.

The federal return does not settle the Montana question. A benefit that is partly taxable on the federal return still goes through Montana's own treatment on the state return. The two results are calculated separately. One does not automatically equal the other.

Older materials may be out of date. Saved worksheets, carried-over tax-software settings and guidance written under the previous method may not reflect how Montana handles benefits now. Anyone relying on those materials should confirm they apply to the 2026 tax year.

The Montana Department of Revenue publishes the state's current income tax forms, instructions and rules. It is the authoritative place to check whether any portion of a benefit is taxable in 2026. Its instructions also explain how a filer's circumstances affect the result.

Residency also shapes the outcome. Montana's treatment of benefits applies to people who are Montana residents for the tax year. A retiree who moves into or out of the state should check which state's rules govern their Social Security income for that year.

New Mexico exempts Social Security benefits from state income tax for single filers with income under $100,000 and joint filers with income under $150,000. The exemption has applied since the 2022 tax year.

The rule works as a threshold test. A retiree whose income stays below the line for their filing status leaves Social Security benefits out of New Mexico taxable income. Filing status decides which of the two lines applies.

The test looks at income, not at the size of the benefit check. Pension payments, retirement account withdrawals and wages can all count toward the limit. A retiree with modest benefits can still lose the exemption if other income pushes the total over the line.

Married couples filing jointly keep the exemption as long as their income stays under $150,000. Single filers must stay under $100,000. The joint line sits $50,000 above the single line, but it is less than double. Two retirees get less combined room as a married couple than they would as two single filers.

Filing status can also change late in life. A surviving spouse who eventually moves from a joint return to a single return is measured against the $100,000 line instead of the $150,000 line. An income that qualified on a joint return can fall outside the exemption on a single return.

These limits sit far above the points where federal tax on benefits begins. A New Mexico retiree can owe federal income tax on part of their Social Security while owing nothing to the state on the same benefits.

Retirees with income at or above those limits are the group New Mexico still taxes on Social Security. For them, the state return generally begins with federal adjusted gross income. That figure already includes the federally taxable share of benefits.

The New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department publishes the current forms and instructions. Retirees close to either line can check them before filing.

Rhode Island exempts Social Security benefits from state income tax only for residents who have reached full retirement age and whose adjusted gross income falls below a state limit. Both conditions must be met. Missing either one leaves the benefits subject to Rhode Island income tax.

The age test ties the exemption to a federal benchmark rather than to a fixed age written into state law. Rhode Island does not set its own retirement age for this purpose. It borrows the one Social Security already uses to calculate benefits.

The Social Security Administration sets full retirement age by birth year. It is 66 for people born from 1943 through 1954. It rises in two-month steps for those born from 1955 through 1959. For anyone born in 1960 or later, it is 67.

That rule matters most for early claimants. Social Security benefits can start as early as age 62, at a permanently reduced amount. For a resident born in 1960 or later, that leaves a five-year stretch between the earliest claiming age and full retirement age. Benefits received during that stretch do not qualify for the state exemption, even when household income is modest.

The second test is income. Rhode Island compares a filer's federal adjusted gross income with a threshold that varies by filing status. The state indexes that threshold to inflation. The dollar limit therefore changes from one tax year to the next. A figure that applied in an earlier year is not a reliable guide to the current one.

Rhode Island's income tax calculation begins with federal adjusted gross income. For residents who miss either test, the federally taxable share of their benefits is the portion that flows into the state return.

The Rhode Island Division of Taxation publishes the current income threshold, along with the instructions for claiming the exemption. Retirees approaching full retirement age, or with income near the limit, can confirm both details there before filing.

Utah includes Social Security benefits in state taxable income, then offsets that tax for many retirees with a nonrefundable Social Security benefit credit. The credit shrinks as income rises and reaches zero for higher-income households.

This works differently from the exemptions and subtractions that several other states use. An exemption or subtraction removes benefits from the income a state taxes. Utah's credit acts on the tax bill instead. The portion of benefits that is taxable at the federal level stays in the income Utah taxes. The credit then lowers the tax that results.

That distinction changes how the relief shows up on a return. A credit reduces the amount of tax owed directly, dollar for dollar. An exemption reduces income instead, and its value depends on the tax rate applied to that income.

Nonrefundable means the credit can bring a person's Utah income tax down to zero but no further. If the credit is larger than the tax owed, the unused portion is not paid out as a refund. A retiree with little or no Utah tax liability therefore gets limited value from the credit. There is little tax for it to offset.

The phaseout ties the credit to income. Households below the point where the phaseout begins can claim the full credit. Above that point, the credit gets smaller as income climbs. At the top of the range it reaches zero, and benefits are taxed without any offset from the credit.

As a result, Utah's treatment of benefits depends on a household's total income, not on the size of its benefits alone. Pension payments, withdrawals from retirement accounts, wages and investment income can all move a household further into the phaseout.

The Utah State Tax Commission publishes the current phaseout thresholds and the instructions for claiming the credit. Retirees can check those figures for the 2026 tax year before estimating what they owe.

Vermont taxes Social Security benefits only for residents whose income rises above a set level. Below that level, benefits are fully exempt from state income tax. Across a middle band of income, known as the phaseout range, the exemption shrinks. Above that band, no exemption applies.

Under this design, total income determines whether Vermont taxes benefits. The benefit amount alone does not. Two retirees who receive identical Social Security payments can land in different parts of the system because of their other income. That income might come from pensions, wages or investments.

The phaseout range works as a sliding scale rather than a single cutoff. A retiree whose income sits near the bottom of the range keeps a larger share of the exemption. A retiree near the top keeps a smaller share. Once income clears the upper end of the range, no exemption remains. Vermont then treats the benefits like other taxable income.

A sliding scale avoids a cliff. With a single cutoff, one extra dollar of income could expose a retiree's entire benefit to state tax. A phaseout spreads that change across a band of income instead.

The design also means a retiree's decisions about other income can affect the state tax on benefits. A larger taxable withdrawal from a retirement account or a return to part-time work raises income. For a retiree inside the phaseout range, that extra income also shrinks the exemption. More of the benefit then becomes taxable in Vermont.

The exemption also works differently from a tax credit. An exemption removes benefit income from the amount the state taxes. A credit reduces the tax bill after it has been calculated.

The Vermont Department of Taxes publishes the current income level for the full exemption and the boundaries of the phaseout range. Those amounts can change from one tax year to the next. The department is the place to confirm the limits for the 2026 tax year before filing.

West Virginia is generally listed as no longer taxing Social Security benefits in 2026. The state taxed benefits in earlier years, then ended that tax through a three-year phaseout that ran through 2026.

That history explains why West Virginia still turns up on some lists of states that tax benefits. Guides written before the phaseout ended included it. A retiree comparing guides from different years may find the state described both ways. The 2026 status is the one that applies to current planning.

A phaseout differs from a one-time repeal. West Virginia did not switch off the tax in a single year. It reduced the tax in stages. The change reached retirees gradually rather than all at once.

The staged design matters for anyone handling a return from an earlier tax year. Each year's return follows the rules in force for that year. A West Virginia resident filing late or amending a return from the phaseout period would apply that year's treatment, not the 2026 one.

The phrase "generally listed" also carries meaning. It reflects how published tax summaries describe the state. Retirees who want certainty about a specific year can confirm the state's treatment with the West Virginia State Tax Department.

The end of the state tax does not change the federal picture. West Virginia residents can still owe federal income tax on part of their benefits. Whether they do depends on their combined income. The repeal removes only the state-level layer of tax on benefits.

The phaseout also covers Social Security benefits specifically. It does not by itself settle how West Virginia treats pensions, retirement account withdrawals or other income. Those follow separate provisions of state tax law.

#5597. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5596. LENDINGTREE REPORTS THIRD QUARTER 2026 RESULTS

Revenue Grew 12% YoY With Increases Across All Three Segments

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LendingTree, Inc. (NASDAQ: TREE), operator of LendingTree.com, the nation's leading online financial services marketplace, today announced results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

The company has posted a letter to shareholders on the company's website at investors.lendingtree.com.

"We are pleased to report our tenth straight quarter of double-digit revenue growth, powered by continued strength in our Insurance segment along with healthy growth in Home driven by great home equity lending results," said Scott Peyree, CEO.  "This quarter we rolled-out AI features and distribution improvements to our shopping experience across multiple product lines.  Specifically, we have implemented voice AI services to help consumers understand and choose the best offer before talking to a lender, AI overviews on offer pages that assist customers in selecting the best offer for their situation, and controlled distribution that helps a consumer shop in stages for a product to prevent multiple carriers or lenders from contacting the customer at once.  Successful expansion of these types of features should ultimately improve consumer satisfaction and drive increased monetization of our traffic."

Jason Bengel, CFO, commented, "The company is on track to grow revenue and AEBITDA this year by 17% and 14%, respectively, at the midpoint of our updated forecast.  Our business benefits from the diversity of our product offering for consumers, providing one unified marketplace for all personal financial products.  This diversification allows us to continue to execute on our growth plan successfully despite ongoing interest rate related headwinds impacting our Home segment.  Our strong results continue to fortify our balance sheet, as we used excess cash to voluntarily repay $60 million of long-term debt during the quarter to improve free cashflow generation for shareholders going forward.  Given the strength of our balance sheet and what we view as attractive valuation of our equity, we intend to repurchase shares during the the fourth quarter for the first time since 1Q22."
