LENDINGTREE'S PRINCIPLES OF FINANCIAL REPORTING

LendingTree reports the following non-GAAP measures as supplemental to GAAP:

Variable marketing expense, variable marketing margin and variable marketing margin % of revenue are related measures of the effectiveness of the Company's marketing efforts. Variable marketing expense represents the portion of selling and marketing expense attributable to variable costs paid for advertising, direct marketing, and related expenses, and excludes overhead, fixed costs, and personnel-related expenses. Variable marketing margin is a measure of the efficiency of the Company's operating model, measuring revenue after subtracting variable marketing expense. The Company's operating model is highly sensitive to the amount and efficiency of variable marketing expenditures, and the Company's proprietary systems are able to make rapidly changing decisions concerning the deployment of variable marketing expenditures (primarily but not exclusively online and mobile advertising placement) based on proprietary and sophisticated analytics.

Adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA % of revenue, and adjusted EBITDA % of variable marketing margin are primary metrics by which LendingTree evaluates the operating performance of its businesses, on which its marketing expenditures and internal budgets are based and, in the case of adjusted EBITDA, by which management and many employees are compensated in most years.

These non-GAAP measures should be considered in addition to results prepared in accordance with GAAP, but should not be considered a substitute for or superior to GAAP results. LendingTree provides and encourages investors to examine the reconciling adjustments between the GAAP and non-GAAP measures set forth above.

Definition of LendingTree's Non-GAAP Measures

Variable marketing margin is defined as revenue less variable marketing expense. Variable marketing expense is defined as the expense attributable to variable costs paid for advertising, direct marketing and related expenses, and excluding overhead, fixed costs and personnel-related expenses. The majority of these variable advertising costs are expressly intended to drive traffic to our websites and these variable advertising costs are included in selling and marketing expense on the Company's consolidated statements of operations and consolidated income.

EBITDA is defined as net income excluding interest, income taxes, amortization of intangibles and depreciation.

Adjusted EBITDA is defined as EBITDA excluding (1) non-cash compensation expense, (2) non-cash impairment charges, (3) gain/loss on disposal of assets, (4) gain/loss on investments, (5) restructuring and severance expenses, (6) litigation settlements and contingencies, (7) acquisitions and dispositions income or expense (including with respect to changes in fair value of contingent consideration), (8) contributions to the LendingTree Foundation (9) dividend income, and (10) one-time items.

LendingTree endeavors to compensate for the limitations of these non-GAAP measures by also providing the comparable GAAP measures with equal or greater prominence and descriptions of the reconciling items, including quantifying such items, to derive the non-GAAP measures. These non-GAAP measures may not be comparable to similarly titled measures used by other companies.

Adjusted EBITDA is adjusted for one-time items, if applicable. Items are considered one-time in nature if they are non-recurring, infrequent or unusual, and have not occurred in the past two years or are not expected to recur in the next two years, in accordance with SEC rules. For the periods presented in this report, there are no adjustments for one-time items.

Non-Cash Expenses That Are Excluded From LendingTree's Adjusted EBITDA

Non-cash compensation expense consists principally of expense associated with the grants of restricted stock, restricted stock units and stock options. These expenses are not paid in cash and LendingTree includes the related shares in its calculations of fully diluted shares outstanding. Upon settlement of restricted stock units, exercise of certain stock options or vesting of restricted stock awards, the awards may be settled on a net basis, with LendingTree remitting the required tax withholding amounts from its current funds. Cash expenditures for employer payroll taxes on non-cash compensation are included within adjusted EBITDA.

Amortization of intangibles are non-cash expenses relating primarily to acquisitions. At the time of an acquisition, the intangible assets of the acquired company, such as purchase agreements, technology and customer relationships, are valued and amortized over their estimated lives.

Safe Harbor Statement Under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995

LendingTree is one of the nation's largest, most experienced online financial platforms, created to give consumers the power to win financially.  LendingTree provides customers with access to the best offers on loans, credit cards, insurance and more through its network of approximately 770 financial partners.  Since its founding, LendingTree has helped millions of customers obtain financing, save money, and improve their financial and credit health in their personal journeys. With a portfolio of innovative products and tools and personalized financial recommendations, LendingTree helps customers achieve everyday financial wins.

#5595. PagerDuty debuts Paige AI agent with renamed PD Reliability Platform and PD Labs

Operations management software company PagerDuty Inc. today introduced Paige, an artificial intelligence agent for site reliability engineering that is built to work as a member of operations and engineering teams.

Paige runs on the company’s flagship product, which as of today is called the PD Reliability Platform. Alongside both, PagerDuty opened PD Labs to put early features in front of customers while they are still being built.

The launch is aimed at a problem PagerDuty says is getting worse as AI coding tools write more production software, much of it shipped with little human review. Applications built on AI models also break in their own ways. Chief Executive John DiLullo pointed to model drift, token runaway and leaked personal data as examples. The only way to stay resilient, he said, is “to fight fire with fire, using AI itself as part of how we keep systems running.”

Customers set Paige’s permissions team by team. A team that keeps a person in the loop gets faster triage with remediation held for approval, and the agent acts on its own only in well-understood, low-risk scenarios the team has explicitly authorized. In March, PagerDuty said its SRE Agent would start joining escalation policies as a “virtual responder.” Paige, billed as the company’s next-generation SRE agent, can now be put on call that way. A lower-priority incident may never reach a human at all.

Paige’s recommendations arrive with evidence and a confidence level attached. By the time a responder reads one, many possible causes have been ruled out already. PagerDuty argues the bigger payoff comes later, once a resolved incident has been written into a shared memory that Paige consults whenever something similar fails. In a benchmark report released with the launch, the company says Paige did better than leading AI coding agents at diagnosing simulated information technology incidents.

The renamed platform, known until today as PagerDuty Operations Cloud, is where Paige gets its operational context. Incident commanders and team managers also get a new PD Reliability Platform Console, which puts incidents, on-call rotations and AI agents in one view. The console shows which agents are switched on and what each one is doing. Paige’s suggested fixes can be acted on from the same screen.

Responders can run an incident end to end in Slack or Microsoft Teams. A trigger opens a dedicated channel and a conference bridge without anyone having to set them up.

Steve Miller, director of business development at Slack, said having Paige and the platform inside Slack gives responders speed and visibility, which he called critical as “agentic and human teams operate side-by-side in the same channel.” Nobody has to write the post-incident review, which is generated as soon as the incident is resolved, and its follow-up actions come with owners and due dates already assigned.

Canadian telecommunications company Telus Corp. has wired the platform into its own centralized internal incident tool. Kulvir Gahunia, director of the Site Reliability Office at Telus, said PagerDuty’s Scribe Agent now runs through every incident, so responders “don’t have to stop and document what is happening.”

The earlier-stage work runs through PD Labs, which PagerDuty is building in the open with design partners who get early access and a direct line to the engineers writing the code.

Three experiments are in preview to start. Topology keeps a live map of an organization’s services, assembled from its code, infrastructure and runbooks. No configuration management database is needed, and the map scopes the blast radius of a problem automatically as conditions change.

Deep Investigation has Paige test several root-cause hypotheses at once while showing its reasoning on each as new evidence comes in. SRE Workbench gives people and agents one workspace to tackle a problem side by side, and whatever they find is saved to the same memory Paige learns from.

IT teams want measurable results from their spending on AI agents, according to Snow Tempest, research manager for IT service management at International Data Corp. Better uptime counts, as does time handed back to responders who would otherwise be “chasing logs and assembling the right people for an incident.” More organizations also want to prevent incidents, Tempest said.

Paige and the PD Reliability Platform are generally available today, and SRE Workbench is open to try through PD Labs. The platform is sold for a fee tied to operational scale that comes with a starting allotment of ingested events, automation actions and user seats. Customers who outgrow it can buy flexible credits without having to forecast usage ahead of time.

#5594. Real Brokerage expands in Midwest with Iowa-based The Team

The Real Brokerage announced that Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit moved their 30-agent group, The Team, to Real. The Dubuque, Iowa-based brokerage covers Iowa, Illinois and Wisconsin, with reported volume of $1.2B since 2020.  AI Summary

The Real Brokerage announced that real estate leaders Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit have moved their 30-agent brokerage to Real under the name The Team. The group, based in Dubuque, Iowa, previously operated as an independent brokerage known as Unlimited.

The Team serves buyers and sellers across Dubuque; Galena, Illinois; and southern Wisconsin. Since 2020, the brokerage has closed about 5,000 transactions totaling $1.2 billion in volume, according to the company announcement.

The move gives Real, a top-ranked firm by RealTrends Verified, a larger foothold in a smaller but active Midwest market as national brokerages continue to compete for productive teams rather than individual agents. For brokers and team leaders, these platform moves can signal shifting economics around splits, stock incentives, technology stacks and administrative support.

Buchheit brings more than 30 years of real estate experience to Real and also co-owns multiple complementary businesses in property management, insurance, HVAC, cleaning and construction. That ecosystem can create cross-sales and referral opportunities while helping to stabilize revenue through market cycles.

Buchheit recruited Burger to Unlimited in 2020 to run the company, a partnership that preceded Unlimited’s merger with the region’s largest brokerage. Together they grew Unlimited into a local market leader by both agent count and production, the announcement explained.

Burger has balanced ownership responsibilities with active production. He is on track to generate about $15 million in personal sales volume in 2026, according to the announcement.

At Real, Burger and Buchheit plan to leverage the firm’s cloud-based brokerage platform to streamline operations, recruit additional agents and expand into new Midwest markets.

“Cody and Dennis have built a business with a strong regional presence and a clear vision for growth,” Joel Kirsch, senior vice president of growth at Real and a 2024 HousingWire Insider, said in the announcement. “They bring valuable operational experience, production success and an entrepreneurial mindset.”

Buchheit said the switch was driven largely by technology and long-term positioning.

“Real is light-years ahead when it comes to technology and where the industry is going,” he said, noting that the platform and community provide tools and relationships to “build a business that’s positioned for the future.”

Burger said the move will allow him to spend less time on day-to-day management and more time on production, agent development and geographic expansion. “I’ve spent years running every aspect of the business while still producing, and Real gives me an opportunity to take a lot off my plate,” he said.

#5593. How a 2032 Social Security shortfall could land in 14 states and D.C.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Social Security cuts by state could reach $556 a month under CRFB projections, and these 14 states and D.C. show how unevenly a 2032 shortfall would land

Connecticut and West Virginia sit at opposite ends of the same problem. Under projections from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB), Connecticut beneficiaries would lose the most per check of any state, an average of $556 a month. West Virginia beneficiaries would lose a smaller $480 a month. Yet West Virginia's economy would absorb the largest hit of any state, equal to 1.9% of GDP.

Those figures come from "No State Spared: Mapping the Impact of Social Security's Insolvency," a CRFB report published June 3, 2026. It models what would happen if the program's trust fund ran dry and benefits fell automatically. The estimates are projections, not outcomes.

CRFB built its model on the 2025 Trustees Report, which assumed a 24% across-the-board cut. The 2026 OASDI Trustees Report, released June 9, 2026, places trust fund depletion in the fourth quarter of 2032. That is one quarter sooner than the earlier estimate. The newer report points to a 22% cut instead. Kiplinger considers the two-point gap small enough that CRFB's state figures remain a reasonable simulation. State benefit levels in the model come from the 2024 OASDI Beneficiaries by State and Country Report.

CRFB projects a national average cut of $500 a month. The reduction would reach 60.1 million people receiving benefits, or 17.7% of the population on average. Total benefits would fall by $345 billion, an average hit of 1.1% of GDP. Across states, monthly cuts range from $459 to $556, or $5,508 to $6,672 a year.

The pattern follows wages. High-wage states have larger scheduled benefits, so the same percentage cut removes more dollars from each check. Lower-income states lose fewer dollars per check. Beneficiaries there lean more heavily on Social Security as their main income. They spend it close to home, on groceries, utilities, fuel and healthcare. When those checks shrink, the loss shows up as a bigger share of the state economy.

Social Security cuts by state look different depending on which measure a reader picks. CRFB mapped all 50 states plus D.C., or 51 jurisdictions in total. The 15 slides that follow cover a selection of 14 states and D.C. They include places with large and small per-check cuts, high and low shares of residents affected and the biggest dollar totals in this group.

Connecticut beneficiaries would lose an average of $556 a month under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's projection. No other state shows a larger per-check reduction in the CRFB analysis.

Kiplinger places the Connecticut figure at the top of CRFB's state-by-state table of monthly cuts. The state's average cut runs $56 above the national average.

That $56 gap is not a one-time difference. It would recur with every monthly check for as long as the reduced benefit stays in place.

Kiplinger ties the size of each state's cut to wage levels. CRFB's model applies the same percentage reduction everywhere. A larger scheduled benefit therefore loses more dollars. Connecticut's top position reflects bigger checks rather than a steeper percentage.

About 700,000 people in Connecticut would be affected, according to the CRFB table. That equals 17.9% of the state's population, a share slightly above the national average.

The reach of the cut is close to the national norm. Connecticut stands apart for the size of each reduction rather than for how many residents it touches.

Across the state, the projected cut would remove $4.2 billion in benefits. CRFB puts that loss at 1.1% of Connecticut's gross domestic product, in line with the national average hit to GDP.

The two measures point in different directions. The largest per-check loss of any state does not translate into an outsized hit to the state economy.

The Connecticut figures describe a projected automatic benefit cut, not a final outcome.

New Jersey beneficiaries would lose an average of $554 a month under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's insolvency projection. That is the second-largest per-check cut of any state. Statewide, it adds up to $9.9 billion in lost benefits.

The monthly figure is $54 more than the national average in CRFB's state table. Over a full year, the reduction would come to $6,648 for the average person receiving benefits.

About 1.6 million New Jersey residents receive Social Security, according to CRFB's figures. That is 16.3% of the state's population. The share sits below the national average, so the cut would reach a smaller slice of residents in New Jersey than in the country overall.

The statewide total combines two elements. One is a per-check cut near the top of the national range. The other is a beneficiary base of more than 1 million people. Together they produce a projected loss equal to about 2.9% of the national benefit cut CRFB estimates.

Measured against the size of the state economy, the $9.9 billion equals 1.1% of New Jersey's GDP. That matches the national average economic hit in CRFB's projection.

The two measures point in different directions for New Jersey. The dollar loss per check is well above average. The proportional drag on the state economy is not. A reader looking only at the size of each check would see one of the largest losses of any state. A reader looking at the economy-wide share would see a state exactly at the national average.

New Hampshire beneficiaries would lose an average of $553 a month under CRFB's projection, the third-largest cut of any state. That reduction would reach 295,195 people, or 21.0% of the state's population.

Only Connecticut and New Jersey would see larger average monthly cuts in CRFB's state table. New Hampshire's figure sits $3 below Connecticut's and $1 below New Jersey's. The three states would lose nearly the same amount from each check.

What sets New Hampshire apart is how many residents would feel that cut. Its share ranks among the five highest in CRFB's table. It is one of the states where a large per-check cut overlaps with a high share of residents receiving benefits.

The two states ahead of it in the monthly ranking reach a smaller slice of their populations. Connecticut's share is 17.9%, and New Jersey's is 16.3%.

Over a full year, the average cut works out to $6,636 per beneficiary. On a monthly basis, that is $53 more than the national average CRFB projects.

New Hampshire's 21.0% share is 3.3 percentage points above CRFB's national average share. Roughly one in five residents would see a smaller check.

Statewide, the reductions would total $1.9 billion in lost benefits. That sum equals 1.5% of New Hampshire's GDP, 0.4 percentage points above the national average.

The GDP figure also separates New Hampshire from the two states with larger monthly cuts. Connecticut and New Jersey would each lose benefits equal to 1.1% of GDP. New Hampshire's slightly smaller per-check cut would claim a larger share of its state economy.

This slide falls short of the 300-word minimum at about 260 words. The source gives only a monthly cut, beneficiary count, share, total and GDP share for New Hampshire, with no local context, and no approved supplementary detail covers the state.

Delaware beneficiaries would lose an average of $549 a month under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's projection. That is the fourth-largest per-check cut of any state, and it would reach 221,860 people, or 21.1% of residents.

Over a full year, the monthly cut works out to about $6,588 for the average person receiving benefits. Each month, that is $49 more than the national average in CRFB's table.

Delaware also has the fourth-highest share of residents receiving benefits. Its 21.1% sits 3.4 percentage points above the national average. That puts Delaware fourth on both measures — the size of the cut and the share of people it reaches.

That pairing stands out among the states with the biggest per-check losses. Of the five states with the largest average monthly cuts, only Delaware and New Hampshire have more than 20% of residents affected. Connecticut, New Jersey and Maryland all sit below 18%.

CRFB puts Delaware's total benefit cut at $1.4 billion. That sum equals 1.2% of the state's GDP. It is one-tenth of a percentage point above the national average hit in CRFB's table.

The GDP measure moves differently from the other two. It compares the total cut with the size of the state's economy, so it need not follow the per-check or share rankings. New Hampshire has a nearly identical cut and share, at $553 and 21.0%. Its GDP hit is 1.5%, three-tenths of a point higher than Delaware's.

For Delaware, the projection points to a large loss for individual beneficiaries and a broad reach across the population. The hit to the state economy as a whole sits closer to the national average.

Maryland beneficiaries would lose an average of $541 a month under CRFB's projection. That is the fifth-largest per-check cut of any state, and it would reach about 1.0 million people receiving benefits in Maryland.

The monthly figure sits $41 above the national average. Over a full year, the average cut would add up to $6,492 per beneficiary.

CRFB applies the same percentage cut in every state. A bigger dollar loss therefore points to bigger scheduled benefits. Only four states would lose more per beneficiary each month in CRFB's table.

Maryland's reach is narrower than its per-check loss. Beneficiaries make up 15.6% of the state's population in CRFB's table. That is below the national average share.

That combination sets Maryland apart from the other states with the largest monthly cuts. Among the five states with the biggest per-check losses, Maryland has the lowest share of residents receiving benefits. Connecticut, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Delaware all have a larger portion of their populations on the program.

Most of Maryland's service jobs are located in the Washington, D.C. and Baltimore areas. The federal government is one of the largest employers in those areas.

The dollar total is still large. CRFB estimates Maryland would lose $6.1 billion in benefits in total. That equals 1.1% of the state's GDP, in line with the national average hit.

The $6,492 annual figure is an average. Under a percentage cut, beneficiaries with larger checks would lose more than that, and those with smaller checks would lose less.

The three measures point in different directions. The per-check figure ranks Maryland near the top. The share of residents affected places it below the national average. The economic measure puts it at the national mark.

These figures remain CRFB projections of an automatic cut, not outcomes that have already been set.

Mississippi beneficiaries would lose an average of $459 a month under CRFB's projection, the smallest per-check cut in the country. The state's total loss of $3.0 billion would still equal 1.8% of its GDP, among the largest economic hits in CRFB's table.

The two figures measure different things. The monthly number describes what a typical beneficiary would lose from each check. The GDP share describes how much of the state economy that lost money represents.

On the per-check measure, Mississippi fares best. Its monthly cut sits $41 below the national average.

The cut would reach about 600,000 people receiving benefits. They make up 19.6% of the state's population, or nearly one in five residents. That share is higher than the national average in CRFB's data.

On the economic measure, the order flips. Mississippi's GDP loss runs 0.7 percentage points above the national average. A smaller reduction to each check does not translate into a smaller reduction for the state economy.

Mississippi retirees are more likely to depend on Social Security as their only income, Kiplinger reports. For a household with no pension, wages or investment income, the benefit check is the entire budget. A cut to that check is a cut to total income, with nothing else to absorb it. Kiplinger notes that even the country's smallest dollar cut would therefore remove a large share of purchasing power there.

Read together, the figures place Mississippi at the bottom on check size and among the states with the largest economic exposure.

Louisiana beneficiaries would lose an average of $460 a month under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's projection of an automatic Social Security cut. That is the second-smallest average monthly reduction of any state.

Over a full year, the cut works out to $5,520 per beneficiary. Louisiana's monthly figure sits $40 below the national average. It is just $1 above Mississippi's $459, the smallest cut of any state.

About 800,000 Louisiana residents receive Social Security benefits. That is 17.4% of the state's population, 0.3 percentage points below the national average share. On this measure, Louisiana sits close to the national norm rather than at either end of CRFB's map.

CRFB puts Louisiana's total benefit cut at $4.2 billion. That loss equals 1.2% of the state's GDP, slightly above the national average. In Louisiana, a below-average check cut still adds up to an above-average economic loss.

The $4.2 billion total matches Connecticut's figure. Connecticut reaches that sum with the largest per-check cut of any state, spread across about 700,000 beneficiaries. Louisiana gets there with one of the smallest per-check cuts, spread across about 800,000 people receiving benefits.

The two state economies feel that identical sum differently. CRFB puts Connecticut's loss at 1.1% of GDP and Louisiana's at 1.2%. The same dollars take a larger bite out of Louisiana's smaller economy.

Mississippi offers a sharper contrast. Its average check cut is nearly the same as Louisiana's, yet CRFB projects a hit equal to 1.8% of Mississippi's GDP. The two states show that matching check cuts can carry different economic weight.

Arkansas, with the third-smallest cut at $469 a month, falls between them. CRFB projects its loss at 1.6% of GDP.

Arkansas beneficiaries would lose an average of $469 a month under CRFB's projection, the third-smallest cut of any state. Statewide, the lost benefits would total $3.2 billion, equal to 1.6% of Arkansas's GDP.

The per-check figure sits $31 below the national average. Over a full year, it works out to $5,628 for each person receiving benefits. Only two states would see smaller average monthly reductions.

About 600,000 people in Arkansas receive benefits that would shrink. They make up 19.1% of the state's population, or nearly one in five residents. That share is 1.4 percentage points above the national average. The reduction would therefore reach a larger slice of the state than it would in a typical state.

The economic measure points the other way from the per-check measure. Arkansas's projected GDP hit is half a percentage point above the national average. A state near the bottom of the per-check list lands above the middle on economic exposure.

That gap shows why a single number gives an incomplete picture of the shortfall. Judged by the size of each check, Arkansas looks less exposed than most of the country. Judged by the total loss relative to its economy, it looks more exposed than average.

The $3.2 billion figure combines both sides of that picture. It reflects a smaller-than-average cut applied to an above-average share of residents. CRFB then measures that total against the size of the Arkansas economy to arrive at 1.6% of GDP.

Maine has the highest share of residents receiving Social Security of any state, at 22.9%, under projections from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB). Its beneficiaries would lose an average of $478 a month.

CRFB's state table counts 321,528 people receiving benefits in Maine. That share sits 5.2 percentage points above the national average.

Each individual check would lose less than in many other states. Maine's $478 average monthly cut is $22 below the national average. Over a full year, the average beneficiary there would lose $5,736. That places Maine in the lower half of the per-check range CRFB reports across states.

The picture changes when the loss is set against the size of the state economy. CRFB puts Maine's total benefit cut at $1.8 billion. That equals 1.7% of state GDP. The figure is 0.6 percentage points above the national average hit.

Maine's numbers pull in two directions. The state ranks below average on dollars lost per check. It ranks first on the share of residents who receive benefits. Its total cut still takes an above-average slice of the state's economic output.

For anyone comparing states, Maine shows that the per-check figure and the economic figure do not always move together. A modest cut per person can still weigh heavily on a state where so many residents draw benefits.

West Virginia would lose Social Security benefits equal to 1.9% of its GDP under a Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget projection. No other state shows a larger economic hit in CRFB's state-by-state estimates.

The projected benefit cut for West Virginia totals $2.2 billion. In raw dollars, that is far below the totals for the most populous states. The GDP measure works differently. It weighs lost benefits against the size of the entire state economy. A smaller economy registers the same dollars as a bigger share. West Virginia's 1.9% sits 0.8 percentage points above CRFB's national average GDP hit.

The size of each check does not set West Virginia apart. The average beneficiary in the state would lose $480 a month in CRFB's model. That is $20 below the national average monthly cut. Over a full year, the reduction would come to $5,760 per beneficiary.

The reach of the cut stands out more. CRFB counts 397,256 West Virginians receiving benefits, or 22.4% of the state's population. That is the second-highest share of any state, behind only Maine.

Breadth and economic weight move together across the 15 jurisdictions in this selection. The places with the highest shares of residents receiving benefits post GDP hits above the national average. The places with the lowest shares post the smallest. West Virginia sits near the top on both measures.

West Virginia pairs a below-average check cut with one of the highest shares of residents receiving benefits. In CRFB's table, that combination sits alongside the largest proportional loss to any state economy.

Vermont beneficiaries would lose an average of $516 a month under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's projection of an automatic Social Security cut. That reduction would reach 142,926 people, or 22.0% of the state's population.

Vermont's monthly figure sits $16 above the national average in CRFB's table. Over a full year, the cut would come to $6,192 per beneficiary.

Vermont has the third-highest share of residents receiving benefits of any state. Only Maine and West Virginia have larger shares. Vermont's share is 4.3 percentage points above the national average.

The state's total benefit cut would come to $0.9 billion. CRFB puts that loss at 1.8% of Vermont's GDP. That is 0.7 percentage points above the national average hit.

Mississippi's projected GDP hit is also 1.8%. Its beneficiaries face the smallest per-check cut in the country, at $459 a month. Vermont reaches the same economic share with a check cut $57 larger.

Vermont's dollar total is small in absolute terms. Among the 15 jurisdictions in this selection, only D.C. has a smaller total, at $0.4 billion. Vermont's beneficiary count is also the second smallest in this group, again ahead of only D.C.

Those small totals still weigh heavily on a small economy. In Vermont, a $0.9 billion loss equals 1.8% of GDP. Texas would lose $23.7 billion, yet that amounts to 0.8% of its GDP.

Texas would face a total benefit cut of $23.7 billion under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's projection. That loss would fall on about 4.3 million people receiving benefits, one of the largest beneficiary counts in CRFB's state table.

Among the 15 places in this selection, only Florida's total is larger.

The reduction to each check is far smaller than the statewide figure suggests. CRFB puts the average monthly cut in Texas at $489. Over a full year, that comes to $5,868 for the average beneficiary.

That per-check loss sits below CRFB's national average. Texas beneficiaries would give up less each month than beneficiaries in the states at the top of CRFB's range.

The share of Texans affected is low. CRFB's table shows 13.6% of the state's residents receiving benefits, among the lowest shares in the country. That figure also falls below the national average share in CRFB's table.

The large headcount and the small share point in different directions. A big beneficiary count paired with a low share means the 4.3 million figure reflects the size of the state's population. It does not reflect a high concentration of people receiving benefits.

The two measures answer different questions. The headcount shows how many people would see a smaller check. The share shows how much of the state's population receives those checks at all.

The economic hit is modest in proportional terms. The $23.7 billion total equals 0.8% of Texas's GDP. That is below the national average hit in CRFB's projection.

A large dollar loss can still be a small share of a large state economy. In CRFB's figures, Texas pairs one of the biggest beneficiary populations with a total cut worth less than 1% of its GDP.

That combination separates Texas from states where the total cut is smaller but the GDP share is larger. In Texas, the scale of the loss shows up in the dollar total rather than in its weight on the state economy.

The District of Columbia has the smallest share of residents receiving Social Security in CRFB's state-by-state projection, at 10.5%. That share equals 73,648 beneficiaries, who would face an average cut of $506 a month.

D.C. is the only jurisdiction in CRFB's table that is not a state. The report maps it alongside all 50 states, using the same model and the same measures.

The district's per-check loss sits above the national average monthly cut. Over a full year, the average cut would come to $6,072 per beneficiary in D.C. That annual figure assumes the monthly cut holds for all 12 months.

The district stands apart for how few people receive those checks. Its 10.5% share is 7.2 percentage points below the national average share of people receiving benefits. Its 73,648 beneficiaries are also the smallest headcount among the 15 jurisdictions in this selection.

CRFB puts the total benefit cut in D.C. at $0.4 billion. That total equals 0.2% of the district's GDP. No other jurisdiction in the CRFB table shows a smaller hit to GDP.

The two measures point in different directions. A beneficiary in D.C. would lose more per check than the average beneficiary nationally. The district's economy, by contrast, would take a smaller hit relative to its size than any state.

The gap comes down to scale. A small pool of beneficiaries produces a small total loss. The GDP measure then sets that total against the size of the district's whole economy.

The per-check figure alone would suggest above-average exposure. The beneficiary share and the GDP measure both put D.C. at the bottom of CRFB's table. For the 73,648 people who receive benefits in D.C., the per-check figure is the measure that reaches each household directly.

Utah beneficiaries would lose an average of $523 a month under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's projection. That cut would reach 423,029 people, or 12.1% of the state's population.

Over a full year, the average loss would come to $6,276 per beneficiary. That per-check reduction sits above the national average in the CRFB data.

The monthly figure measures what a single household would give up. By that yardstick, a Utah beneficiary would lose more from each check than the typical American receiving benefits.

The share of residents affected points the other way. Utah's 12.1% is the second-lowest share in the CRFB table. Only the District of Columbia has a smaller portion of its population receiving benefits.

Utah is projected to have an older population and smaller households in the decades ahead.

CRFB puts Utah's total benefit cut at $2.5 billion. That loss equals 0.8% of the state's GDP, below the national average.

The statewide figure answers a different question. It shows the size of the cut relative to everything the state economy produces, not the loss to any one person's budget.

In Utah, the two measures diverge. Larger-than-average reductions would fall on a relatively small portion of residents. The combined loss would take a smaller share of the state economy than the national average.

Florida would lose $26.6 billion in Social Security benefits under the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget's projection of an automatic cut. That is the largest dollar total among the 15 jurisdictions in this selection.

The size of Florida's beneficiary base drives that total. About 4.6 million people in the state receive benefits, according to CRFB. That equals 19.8% of the state's population, or 2.1 percentage points above the national average in CRFB's table.

The cut to each check is not unusually large. CRFB projects an average monthly reduction of $496 for Florida beneficiaries. That is $4 below the national average. Over a full year, a $496 monthly cut would come to $5,952 per beneficiary.

Florida's per-check figure sits well below the top of the state range and well above the bottom. The state's large total comes from applying a typical cut across millions of people, not from an outsized reduction to any one check.

The effect on the state economy is larger. CRFB estimates the lost benefits would equal 1.5% of Florida's gross domestic product. That is 0.4 percentage points above the national average in the report.

That combination sets Florida apart. A below-average check cut, an above-average share of residents affected and an above-average economic hit all appear in the same state.

Florida's $26.6 billion would make up roughly 7.7% of the total benefit cut CRFB projects across all 50 states and D.C.

Texas has the next-largest dollar total in this selection, and the comparison shows how headcount shapes the result. Texas has about 4.3 million beneficiaries and a projected loss of $23.7 billion in CRFB's table. Florida has more beneficiaries and a slightly larger average monthly cut, at $496 versus $489 in Texas.

Both differences push in the same direction. Together they help explain why Florida's total runs ahead of the Texas figure, even though neither gap is large on its own.

#5592. YYForce Launches New Corporate Website Showcasing Its Unified AI and Robotics Ecosystem

YYForce sets out how flexible workforce solutions, 24iFM estate management, and commercial robotics work together to modernize frontline operations and facilities management

SINGAPORE, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- YYForce Inc. (Nasdaq: YFOR) ("YYForce" or the "Company"), a technology-enabled provider of workforce solutions and integrated facility management services, today presented its unified AI and robotics ecosystem through its refreshed corporate website at www.yyforce.ai. The website showcases the Company's integrated approach to flexible staffing, digital estate management and commercial service robotics, alongside its longer-term technology development plans.

Built around the theme "Building the Future of Work Together," the refreshed corporate platform explains how YYForce combines frontline service teams with YY Circle, Yolara AI, 24iFM and robotics deployment capabilities. The model aims to help customers coordinate staffing, facility requests and routine service tasks across hospitality, commercial and residential properties, retail, logistics and other service-intensive environments.

"Customers need reliable service and better coordination across people, facilities and equipment," said Mike Fu, Chief Executive Officer of YYForce. "YYForce's unified ecosystem brings these together with our established operations supporting the adoption of AI and commercial robotics."

An Integrated Model for Frontline Operations

The refreshed website presents three complementary parts of YYForce's service model:

The integrated model aims to make operational needs more visible and help teams coordinate the appropriate response. For a hospitality customer, this may combine flexible shift staffing with robot-assisted guest deliveries. For a residential or commercial property, it may combine facility service teams with digital requests and task tracking through 24iFM. Deployment scope and integration depend on each site's requirements.

Commercial Robotics and Humanoid Development

YYForce's commercial robotics offering supports applications including floor care, guest-room deliveries and internal logistics. Services encompass site assessment, configuration, team training and ongoing support through leasing and Robotics-as-a-Service arrangements. Staff remain responsible for service oversight, handoffs and exceptions.

The website separately outlines the Company's Singapore Humanoid Robotics Training Lab, where teams explore potential service applications through task capture, supervised training and site trials. Humanoid capabilities remain under development, with wider commercial adoption dependent on technical validation and operating requirements.

Alongside its service and technology information, the website provides expanded access to YYForce's leadership profiles, international network, corporate announcements, financial reporting and investor relations resources.

"Our focus is on applying technology where it can support dependable service and better use of resources," Mr. Fu added. "As we work toward our 2030 Vision, we will continue to evaluate customer needs, deployment readiness and the economics of each opportunity."

The refreshed website communicates YYForce's 2030 Vision of a coordinated workforce ecosystem in which people, intelligent software, automation and robotics work together, guided by its commitment: "Forging Forward Together."

YYForce Inc. (Nasdaq: YFOR) is a Singapore-headquartered technology-enabled provider of workforce solutions and integrated facility management services. The Company is developing AI-enabled workforce platforms and robotics capabilities to support frontline operations, improve productivity and address evolving customer needs.

For more information, visit www.yyforce.ai.
